title: Accelerated Profile HMM Searches
abstract: Profile hidden Markov models (profile HMMs) and probabilistic inference methods have made important contributions to the theory of sequence database homology search. However, practical use of profile HMM methods has been hindered by the computational expense of existing software implementations. Here I describe an acceleration heuristic for profile HMMs, the "multiple segment Viterbi" (MSV) algorithm. The MSV algorithm computes an optimal sum of multiple ungapped local alignment segments using a striped vector-parallel approach previously described for fast Smith/Waterman alignment. MSV scores follow the same statistical distribution as gapped optimal local alignment scores, allowing rapid evaluation of significance of an MSV score and thus facilitating its use as a heuristic filter. I also describe a 20-fold acceleration of the standard profile HMM Forward/Backward algorithms using a method I call "sparse rescaling". These methods are assembled in a pipeline in which high-scoring MSV hits are passed on for reanalysis with the full HMM Forward/Backward algorithm. This accelerated pipeline is implemented in the freely available HMMER3 software package. Performance benchmarks show that the use of the heuristic MSV filter sacrifices negligible sensitivity compared to unaccelerated profile HMM searches. HMMER3 is substantially more sensitive and 100- to 1000-fold faster than HMMER2. HMMER3 is now about as fast as BLAST for protein searches.
summary:
Title: Revolutionizing Sequence Database Homology Search: Accelerated Profile HMM Searches

In a groundbreaking development, Computer Science researcher Sean R. Eddy has introduced an acceleration heuristic for Profile Hidden Markov Models (profile HMMs) in the journal PLoS Computational Biology. Known as the "Multiple Segment Viterbi" (MSV) algorithm, this new method speeds up computations that had previously slowed down practical applications of profile HMM methods.

The MSV algorithm, built upon a striped vector-parallel approach for fast Smith/Waterman alignment, calculates optimal ungapped local alignments swiftly. Scores obtained from the MSV algorithm follow the same statistical distribution as those from gapped optimal local alignment scores, making it possible to quickly assess their significance and use them as a heuristic filter.

To further enhance the speed of profile HMM searches, Eddy also presents a 20-fold acceleration method termed "sparse rescaling" for the standard Forward/Backward algorithms. These optimizations are integrated into the newly released HMMER3 software package, promising greater sensitivity and significantly faster speeds than its predecessor, HMMER2. With HMMER3, protein searches are now as swift as with BLAST, marking a significant stride in computational biology.

title: Wetting: statics and dynamics
abstract: The wetting of solids by liquids is connected to physical chemistry (wettability), to statistical physics (pinning of the contact line, wetting transitions, etc.), to long-range forces (van der Waals, double layers), and to fluid dynamics. The present review represents an attempt towards a unified picture with special emphasis on certain features of "dry spreading": (a) the final state of a spreading droplet need not be a monomolecular film; (b) the spreading drop is surrounded by a precursor film, where most of the available free energy is spent; and (c) polymer melts may slip on the solid and belong to a separate dynamical class, conceptually related to the spreading of superfluids.
summary:
Title: Unifying Wetting Science: A Comprehensive Review

In a groundbreaking study published in Reviews of Modern Physics, acclaimed scientist P. G. de Gennes delves into the complex and multidisciplinary field of wetting. The paper, titled "Wetting: Static and Dynamics," brings together several key disciplines — physical chemistry, statistical physics, fluid dynamics, and even aspects from physics — to create a cohesive understanding of how liquids interact with solids.

De Gennes' review focuses on certain unique aspects of "dry spreading," including the unexpected final states of spreading droplets and the significant energy spent in precursor films. Additionally, the study highlights the role of polymer melts, which may exhibit unique slippage behavior on solids and belong to a separate dynamical class akin to that of superfluids. This work aims to provide a unified framework for the dynamic and intricate phenomena involved in wetting.

summary:
**New research breakthrough: Ageneral expression for linear potential sweep voltammogram in diffusionless systems**

In a groundbreaking study published in the Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry, chemist E. Laviron provides an expression for linear potential sweep voltammetry, offering insight into electrochemical reactions where diffusion plays a minimal role. This work extends our understanding of coulometry and voltammetry, essential tools in non-diffusion-controlled electrochemistry, contributing significantly to future advancements in this field.

title: Smoothed particle hydrodynamics: theory and application to non-spherical stars
abstract: A new hydrodynamic code applicable to a space of an arbitrary number of dimensions is discussed and applied to a variety of polytropic stellar models. The principal feature of the method is the use of statistical techniques to recover analytical expressions for the physical variables from a known distribution of fluid elements. The equations of motion take the form of Newtonian equations for particles. Starting with a non-axisymmetric distribution of approximately 80 particles in three dimensions, the method is found to reproduce the structure of uniformly rotating and magnetic polytropes to within a few per cent. The method may be easily extended to deal with more complicated physical models.
summary:
**Astronomy Advancement: Revolutionary Hydrodynamic Code Aids Study of Non-Spherical Stars**

In a groundbreaking study published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, physicists R. A. Gingold and J. J. Monaghan present a new hydrodynamic code suitable for multidimensional space analysis. The innovative technique uses statistical methods to reconstruct physical variables from fluid elements' distribution, resembling Newtonian particle equations in motion.

Applied to various polytropic stellar models, this method shows promising accuracy, accurately reproducing the structure of rotating and magnetized polytropes with errors under 5%. This new approach could streamline more complex physical models studying in astronomy's future.

title: Development of a turbulence closure model for geophysical fluid problems
abstract: Applications of second‐moment turbulent closure hypotheses to geophysical fluid problems have developed rapidly since 1973, when genuine predictive skill in coping with the effects of stratification was demonstrated. The purpose here is to synthesize and organize material that has appeared in a number of articles and add new useful material so that a complete (and improved) description of a turbulence model from conception to application is condensed in a single article. It is hoped that this will be a useful reference to users of the model for application to either atmospheric or oceanic boundary layers.
summary: In the field of geophysics, a groundbreaking paper by Mellor and Yamada published in Reviews of Geophysics presents a significant advancement in turbulence modeling for geophysical fluid problems. Building upon prior research from 1973 that demonstrated genuine predictive skill in managing the effects of stratification, this study aims to provide a comprehensive synthesis of the evolving second-moment turbulent closure hypotheses. The authors offer new insight and tools, streamlining the process from concept development to practical application, with implications for both atmospheric and oceanic boundary layers. This work could potentially shape future studies in geophysical fluid dynamics by offering a more cohesive and accessible resource for turbulence modeling.

title: Significance of Electromagnetic Potentials in the Quantum Theory
abstract: In this paper, we discuss some interesting properties of the electromagnetic potentials in the quantum domain. We shall show that, contrary to the conclusions of classical mechanics, there exist effects of potentials on charged particles, even in the region where all the fields (and therefore the forces on the particles) vanish. We shall then discuss possible experiments to test these conclusions; and, finally, we shall suggest further possible developments in the interpretation of the potentials.
summary:
Paper Title: Unexpected Electromagnetic Effects in Quantum Realm Uncovered

New paper published in Physical Review by Yakir Aharonov and David Böhm reveals intriguing properties of electromagnetic potentials within quantum mechanics. Contrary to classical mechanics, the research suggests that electromagnetic potentials can influence charged particles, even where all fields and therefore forces on the particles are absent. Potential experiments to test these findings are being proposed, and the authors also suggest further interpretations of how these discoveries could shape our understanding of quantum mechanics.

title: On Gauge Invariance and Vacuum Polarization
abstract: This paper is based on the elementary remark that the extraction of gauge invariant results from a formally gauge invariant theory is ensured if one employs methods of solution that involve only gauge covariant quantities. We illustrate this statement in connection with the problem of vacuum polarization by a prescribed electromagnetic field. The vacuum current of a charged Dirac field, which can be expressed in terms of the Green's function of that field, implies an addition to the action integral of the electromagnetic field. Now these quantities can be related to the dynamical properties of a "particle" with space-time coordinates that depend upon a proper-time parameter. The proper-time equations of motion involve only electromagnetic field strengths, and provide a suitable gauge invariant basis for treating problems. Rigorous solutions of the equations of motion can be obtained for a constant field, and for a plane wave field. A renormalization of field strength and charge, applied to the modified lagrange function for constant fields, yields a finite, gauge invariant result which implies nonlinear properties for the electromagnetic field in the vacuum. The contribution of a zero spin charged field is also stated. After the same field strength renormalization, the modified physical quantities describing a plane wave in the vacuum reduce to just those of the maxwell field; there are no nonlinear phenomena for a single plane wave, of arbitrary strength and spectral composition. The results obtained for constant (that is, slowly varying fields), are then applied to treat the two-photon disintegration of a spin zero neutral meson arising from the polarization of the proton vacuum. We obtain approximate, gauge invariant expressions for the effective interaction between the meson and the electromagnetic field, in which the nuclear coupling may be scalar, pseudoscalar, or pseudovector in nature. The direct verification of equivalence between the pseudoscalar and pseudovector interactions only requires a proper statement of the limiting processes involved. For arbitrarily varying fields, perturbation methods can be applied to the equations of motion, as discussed in Appendix A, or one can employ an expansion in powers of the potential vector. The latter automatically yields gauge invariant results, provided only that the proper-time integration is reserved to the last. This indicates that the significant aspect of the proper-time method is its isolation of divergences in integrals with respect to the proper-time parameter, which is independent of the coordinate system and of the gauge. The connection between the proper-time method and the technique of "invariant regularization" is discussed. Incidentally, the probability of actual pair creation is obtained from the imaginary part of the electromagnetic field action integral. Finally, as an application of the Green's function for a constant field, we construct the mass operator of an electron in a weak, homogeneous external field, and derive the additional spin magnetic moment of $\frac{\ensuremath{\alpha}}{2\ensuremath{\pi}}$ magnetons by means of a perturbation calculation in which proper-mass plays the customary role of energy.
summary:
In a groundbreaking paper published in Physical Review, physicist Julian Schwinger advances our understanding of gauge theory and vacuum polarization. The study demonstrates that employing methods involving only gauge covariant quantities ensures the extraction of gauge-invariant results from a formally gauge-invariant theory.

To illustrate this principle, Schwinger tackles the problem of vacuum polarization by a prescribed electromagnetic field, deriving an addition to the action integral of the electromagnetic field that involves dynamical properties of "particles" with space-time coordinates dependent on a proper-time parameter. Through intricate calculations for constant and plane wave fields, the paper reveals nonlinear properties for the electromagnetic field in the vacuum and provides gauge invariant expressions for two-photon disintegration of a spin-zero neutral meson arising from proton vacuum polarization. The work suggests connections to the "invariant regularization" technique and offers insights into the probability of pair creation. Overall, this research lays an essential foundation for understanding complex interactions within the electromagnetic field.

title: An Alternative to Compactification
abstract: Conventional wisdom states that Newton's force law implies only four noncompact dimensions. We demonstrate that this is not necessarily true in the presence of a nonfactorizable background geometry. The specific example we study is a single 3-brane embedded in five dimensions. We show that even without a gap in the Kaluza-Klein spectrum, four-dimensional Newtonian and general relativistic gravity is reproduced to more than adequate precision.
summary:
Title: New Study Suggests Possible Alteration to Four-Dimensional Physics

Journal: Physical Review Letters
Authors: Lisa Randall & Raman Sundrum

The scientists, Lisa Randall and Raman Sundrum, have proposed an alternative to the notion that Newton's force law only allows for four noncompact dimensions in physics. This challenge to conventional wisdom comes from the presence of a nonfactorizable background geometry, as demonstrated by studying a single 3-brane embedded in five dimensions. Surprisingly, even without a gap in the Kaluza-Klein spectrum, the researchers have managed to reproduce four-dimensional Newtonian and general relativistic gravity with impressive precision. This work could open new avenues for understanding physics beyond the familiar four dimensions.

title: A new integral equation formalism for the polarizable continuum model: Theoretical background and applications to isotropic and anisotropic dielectrics
abstract: We present a new integral equation formulation of the polarizable continuum model (PCM) which allows one to treat in a single approach dielectrics of different nature: standard isotropic liquids, intrinsically anisotropic medialike liquid crystals and solid matrices, or ionic solutions. The present work shows that integral equation methods may be used with success also for the latter cases, which are usually studied with three-dimensional methods, by far less competitive in terms of computational effort. We present the theoretical bases which underlie the method and some numerical tests which show both a complete equivalence with standard PCM versions for isotropic solvents, and a good efficiency for calculations with anisotropic dielectrics.
summary:
New Integral Equation Method for Polarizable Continuum Model Offers Flexibility for Various Dielectric Materials

In a new study published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, researchers led by Éric Cancès present a novel integral equation formalism for the polarizable continuum model (PCM). This innovative method can treat dielectrics of various natures, including standard isotropic liquids, anisotropic media like liquid crystals, and solid matrices or ionic solutions.

The study demonstrates that integral equation methods are not only suitable for isotropic solvents but can also handle more complex anisotropic dielectrics, usually studied with computationally intensive three-dimensional methods. The researchers provide theoretical foundations for the method and conduct numerical tests confirming its equivalence to standard PCM versions for isotropic solvents and efficiency for calculations involving anisotropic dielectrics.

title: Social force model for pedestrian dynamics
abstract: It is suggested that the motion of pedestrians can be described as if they would be subject to ``social forces.'' These ``forces'' are not directly exerted by the pedestrians' personal environment, but they are a measure for the internal motivations of the individuals to perform certain actions (movements). The corresponding force concept is discussed in more detail and can also be applied to the description of other behaviors. In the presented model of pedestrian behavior several force terms are essential: first, a term describing the acceleration towards the desired velocity of motion; second, terms reflecting that a pedestrian keeps a certain distance from other pedestrians and borders; and third, a term modeling attractive effects. The resulting equations of motion of nonlinearly coupled Langevin equations. Computer simulations of crowds of interacting pedestrians show that the social force model is capable of describing the self-organization of several observed collective effects of pedestrian behavior very realistically.
summary: In physics journal "Physical Review E," researchers Dirk Helbing and Péter Molnár propose a new way to explain pedestrian dynamics using a Social Force Model. This model suggests individuals in crowds move as if they are influenced by "social forces," internal motivations driving movements rather than external factors. The model includes terms for desired velocity, personal space maintenance, and attraction, which when combined create striking simulations of crowd behaviors and self-organization.
journal: Physical review. E, Statistical physics, plasmas, fluids, and related interdisciplinary topics

title: Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I.
abstract: Examples of coupled irreversible processes like the thermoelectric phenomena, the transference phenomena in electrolytes and heat conduction in an anisotropic medium are considered. For certain cases of such interaction reciprocal relations have been deduced by earlier writers, e.g., Thomson's theory of thermoelectric phenomena and Helmholtz' theory for the e.m.f. of electrolytic cells with liquid junction. These earlier derivations may be classed as quasi-thermodynamic; in fact, Thomson himself pointed out that his argument was incomplete, and that his relation ought to be established on an experimental basis. A general class of such relations will be derived by a new theoretical treatment from the principle of microscopic reversibility. (\textsection{}\textsection{}1-2.) The analogy with a chemical monomolecular triangle reaction is discussed; in this case a a simple kinetic consideration assuming microscopic reversibility yields a reciprocal relation that is not necessary for fulfilling the requirements of thermodynamics (\textsection{}3). Reciprocal relations for heat conduction in an anisotropic medium are derived from the assumption of microscopic reversibility, applied to fluctuations. (\textsection{}4.) The reciprocal relations can be expressed in terms of a potential, the dissipation-function. Lord Rayleigh's "principle of the least dissipation of energy" is generalized to include the case of anisotropic heat conduction. A further generalization is announced. (\textsection{}5.) The conditions for stationary flow are formulated; the connection with earlier quasi-thermodynamic theories is discussed. (\textsection{}6.) The principle of dynamical reversibility does not apply when (external) magnetic fields or Coriolis forces are present, and the reciprocal relations break down. (\textsection{}7.)
summary:
Title: New Physics Theory Reveals Reciprocity in Irreversible Processes

The Physical Review publishes a groundbreaking paper by Lars Onsager, titled "Reciprocal Relations in Irreversible Processes. I." The work explores the phenomenon of coupled irreversible processes in physics and expands upon prior theories such as Thomson's theory of thermoelectric phenomena and Helmholtz' theory for electrolytic cells with a liquid junction. According to Onsager, these earlier derivations were quasi-thermodynamic and incomplete, requiring experimental confirmation.

The paper introduces a new theoretical approach that derives reciprocal relations using the principle of microscopic reversibility, which can be applied to various processes including thermal conduction in anisotropic media and chemical monomolecular triangle reactions. The findings are significant as they help establish the general dynamics of these complex interactions, offering insight into thermal conduction, electrochemistry, and even potential applications in energy conservation.

The work also addresses the implications of stationary flow, magnetic fields, and Coriolis forces on the reciprocal relations, adding to the understanding of thermodynamics and its connection with real-world phenomena. The article concludes by generalizing Lord Rayleigh's principle of the least dissipation of energy for anisotropic heat conduction, announcing a further significant generalization soon to follow.

title: On the identification of a vortex
abstract: Considerable confusion surrounds the longstanding question of what constitutes a vortex, especially in a turbulent flow. This question, frequently misunderstood as academic, has recently acquired particular significance since coherent structures (CS) in turbulent flows are now commonly regarded as vortices. An objective definition of a vortex should permit the use of vortex dynamics concepts to educe CS, to explain formation and evolutionary dynamics of CS, to explore the role of CS in turbulence phenomena, and to develop viable turbulence models and control strategies for turbulence phenomena. We propose a definition of a vortex in an incompressible flow in terms of the eigenvalues of the symmetric tensor ${\bm {\cal S}}^2 + {\bm \Omega}^2$ ; here ${\bm {\cal S}}$ and ${\bm \Omega}$ are respectively the symmetric and antisymmetric parts of the velocity gradient tensor ${\bm \Delta}{\bm u}$ . This definition captures the pressure minimum in a plane perpendicular to the vortex axis at high Reynolds numbers, and also accurately defines vortex cores at low Reynolds numbers, unlike a pressure-minimum criterion. We compare our definition with prior schemes/definitions using exact and numerical solutions of the Euler and Navier–Stokes equations for a variety of laminar and turbulent flows. In contrast to definitions based on the positive second invariant of ${\bm \Delta}{\bm u}$ or the complex eigenvalues of ${\bm \Delta}{\bm u}$ , our definition accurately identifies the vortex core in flows where the vortex geometry is intuitively clear.
summary:
New Study Clarifies Definition of Vortices in Turbulent Flows

In a groundbreaking paper published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics, researchers Jinhee Jeong and Fazle Hussain have proposed a new definition for vortices in incompressible flow, aiming to bring clarity to a long-debated question within physics. The study seeks to explain the formation and evolutionary dynamics of coherent structures (CS) in turbulent flows, key components now commonly regarded as vortices, with applications for developing novel turbulence models and control strategies.

The authors suggest defining vortices based on the eigenvalues of the symmetric tensor ${\bm {\cal S}}^2 + {\bm \Omega}^2$, using the symmetric (${\bm {\cal S}}$) and antisymmetric (${\bm \Omega}$) parts of the velocity gradient tensor (${\bm \Delta}{\bm u}$). The new definition accurately identifies vortex cores in flows where geometry is intuitively clear, outperforming prior schemes such as those based on the positive second invariant of ${\bm \Delta}{\bm u}$ or complex eigenvalues of ${\bm \Delta}{\bm u}$. This work offers promising insights for advancing our understanding of turbulence phenomena and potentially contributing to future turbulence modeling and control efforts.

title: The hierarchy problem and new dimensions at a millimeter
abstract: We propose a new framework for solving the hierarchy problem which does not rely on either supersymmetry or technicolor. In this framework, the gravitational and gauge interactions become united at the weak scale, which we take as the only fundamental short distance scale in nature. The observed weakness of gravity on distances ≳ 1 mm is due to the existence of n≥2 new compact spatial dimensions large compared to the weak scale. The Planck scale MPl∼GN−1/2 is not a fundamental scale; its enormity is simply a consequence of the large size of the new dimensions. While gravitons can freely propagate in the new dimensions, at sub-weak energies the Standard Model (SM) fields must be localized to a 4-dimensional manifold of weak scale “thickness” in the extra dimensions. This picture leads to a number of striking signals for accelerator and laboratory experiments. For the case of n=2 new dimensions, planned sub-millimeter measurements of gravity may observe the transition from 1/r2→1/r4 Newtonian gravitation. For any number of new dimensions, the LHC and NLC could observe strong quantum gravitational interactions. Furthermore, SM particles can be kicked off our 4 dimensional manifold into the new dimensions, carrying away energy, and leading to an abrupt decrease in events with high transverse momentum pT≳ TeV. For certain compact manifolds, such particles will keep circling in the extra dimensions, periodically returning, colliding with and depositing energy to our four dimensional vacuum with frequencies of ∼1012 Hz or larger. As a concrete illustration, we construct a model with SM fields localized on the 4-dimensional throat of a vortex in 6 dimensions, with a Pati-Salam gauge symmetry SU(4)×SU(2)×SU(2) in the bulk.
summary:
Title: Unraveling New Dimensions to Solve the Gravity Hierarchy Problem

Newspaper Article:

A groundbreaking paper by physicists Nima Arkani–Hamed, Savas Dimopoulos, and G. Dvali proposes a revolutionary framework to address the long-standing Hierarchy Problem in physics. Abandoning the reliance on supersymmetry or technicolor, this new theory unites gravitational and gauge interactions at the weak scale. The authors suggest that gravity's apparent weakness beyond distances of 1 millimeter arises from the presence of multiple extra spatial dimensions larger than the weak scale.

This intriguing premise implies that the Planck scale, traditionally considered a fundamental scale, is actually an outcome of the expansion of these new dimensions. The proposed model also presents compelling opportunities for discoveries in accelerator and laboratory experiments — sub-millimeter gravity measurements could reveal a shift from 1/r² to 1/r⁴ Newtonian gravitation for the case of two additional dimensions.

In addition, this innovative theory opens up possibilities for both the LHC and NLC to detect strong quantum gravitational interactions. The authors further propose that Standard Model particles could periodically escape into these extra dimensions, potentially leading to a surge in high-energy events and collisions with subsequent energy deposition back in our four-dimensional vacuum at frequencies as high as 10¹² Hz or more.

title: Elastic Properties of Lipid Bilayers: Theory and Possible Experiments
abstract: Abstract A theory of the elasticity of lipid bilayers is proposed. Three types of strain, i. e. stretching, tilt and curvature, are distinguished and the associated stresses are identified. It is argued that in the case of vesicles (= closed bilayer films) the only elasticity controlling nonspherical shapes is that of curvature. Euler-Lagrange equations are derived for the shape in magnetic fields and under excess outside pressure. It is shown that magnetic fields can deform spherical vesicles into ellipsoids of revolution. Under excess outside pressure the spherical shape becomes unstable at a certain threshold pressure. Both effects can be influenced by a spontaneous curvature of the bilayer. Some possible experiments to determine the elastic properties are also discussed
summary:
New Study Sheds Light on Elastic Properties of Lipid Bilayers

In a new paper published in Zeitschrift für Naturforschung C, researcher W. Helfrich proposes a theory on the elasticity of lipid bilayers, highlighting three strains: stretching, tilt, and curvature. According to the study, vesicles - or closed bilayer films - are primarily affected by the elasticity of curvature when it comes to non-spherical shapes. The findings suggest that magnetic fields can deform spherical vesicles into ellipsoids of revolution and reveal the point at which spherical shapes become unstable under excess outside pressure. Furthermore, the work presents possibilities for future experiments to determine lipid bilayer elastic properties. Overall, this study contributes to classical mechanics research around lipid bilayers.

title: Theory of open quantum systems
abstract: A quantum dissipation theory is constructed with the system–bath interaction being treated rigorously at the second-order cumulant level for both reduced dynamics and initial canonical boundary condition. The theory is valid for arbitrary bath correlation functions and time-dependent external driving fields, and satisfies correlated detailed-balance relation at any temperatures. The general formulation assumes a particularly simple form in driven Brownian oscillator systems in which the correlated driving-dissipation effects can be accounted for exactly in terms of local-field correction. Remarks on a class of widely used phenomenological quantum master equations that neglects the bath dispersion-induced dissipation are also made in contact with the present theory.
summary:
New Quantum Dissipation Theory Offers Insights into Open Systems

In a groundbreaking paper published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, authors Rui–Xue Xu and YiJing Yan have developed a comprehensive quantum dissipation theory. This new approach is significant as it treats the system-bath interaction rigorously, providing a solution for arbitrarily correlated bath functions and time-dependent external driving fields while maintaining balance at any temperatures.

The theory, applicable to diverse quantum systems, also simplifies in the context of driven Brownian oscillators due to its ability to address correlated driving-dissipation effects precisely through local-field corrections. The paper additionally offers insights into popular phenomenological quantum master equations that have overlooked dispersion-induced dissipation, providing a deeper understanding within the broader field of statistical physics and physics.

title: DYNAMICS OF DARK ENERGY
abstract: We review in detail a number of approaches that have been adopted to try and explain the remarkable observation of our accelerating universe. In particular we discuss the arguments for and recent progress made towards understanding the nature of dark energy. We review the observational evidence for the current accelerated expansion of the universe and present a number of dark energy models in addition to the conventional cosmological constant, paying particular attention to scalar field models such as quintessence, K-essence, tachyon, phantom and dilatonic models. The importance of cosmological scaling solutions is emphasized when studying the dynamical system of scalar fields including coupled dark energy. We study the evolution of cosmological perturbations allowing us to confront them with the observation of the Cosmic Microwave Background and Large Scale Structure and demonstrate how it is possible in principle to reconstruct the equation of state of dark energy by also using Supernovae Ia observational data. We also discuss in detail the nature of tracking solutions in cosmology, particle physics and braneworld models of dark energy, the nature of possible future singularities, the effect of higher order curvature terms to avoid a Big Rip singularity, and approaches to modifying gravity which leads to a late-time accelerated expansion without recourse to a new form of dark energy.
summary:
Title: New Approaches to Unraveling the Mystery of Dark Energy

Subheading: A Review of Different Theories Proposing solutions for our Accelerating Universe

In an intriguing turn of events, physicists Edmund J. Copeland, M. Sami, and Shinji Tsujikawa have reviewed various strategies aimed at solving the perplexing conundrum of a universe that's expanding at an accelerated rate (International Journal of Modern Physics D). The researchers focus on exploring the nature of dark energy, an elusive force thought to be driving this expansion.

Notably, they delve into debates surrounding conventional theories like the cosmological constant, while paying special attention to more complex scalar field models such as quintessence and K-essence, tachyon, phantom, and dilatonic models. Furthermore, they discuss the importance of cosmological scaling solutions in analyzing diverse systems involving scalar fields, including coupled dark energy (International Journal of Modern Physics D).

The team also examines the evolution of cosmic perturbations to compare with observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background and Large Scale Structure. Through their work, they demonstrate that in principle, data from Supernovae Ia can potentially reveal the equation of state for dark energy. Lastly, they delve into the nature of tracking solutions, future singularities, higher order curvature terms to avoid a Big Rip singularity, and modifications in gravity, all leading to late-time accelerated expansions without requiring novel forms of dark energy (International Journal of Modern Physics D).

title: Nominal Rigidities and the Dynamic Effects of a Shock to Monetary Policy
abstract: We present a model embodying moderate amounts of nominal rigidities that accounts for the observed inertia in inflation and persistence in output. The key features of our model are those that prevent a sharp rise in marginal costs after an expansionary shock to monetary policy. Of these features, the most important are staggered wage contracts that have an average duration of three quarters and variable capital utilization.
summary:
Economic Study Offers Insights on Monetary Policy Shock Effects

Evans present a model that explains observed persistence in inflation and output after an expansionary monetary policy shock. The model emphasizes nominal rigidities that prevent a sudden increase in marginal costs following the shock. Key features include staggered wage contracts with an average duration of three quarters, as well as variable capital utilization. These mechanisms contribute to the inertia in inflation and persistence in output, shedding light on the dynamics of monetary policy's impact on the economy.

title: On the Temperature Dependence of Cooperative Relaxation Properties in Glass-Forming Liquids
abstract: A molecular-kinetic theory, which explains the temperature dependence of relaxation behavior in glass-forming liquids in terms of the temperature variation of the size of the cooperatively rearranging region, is presented. The size of this cooperatively rearranging region is shown to be determined by configuration restrictions in these glass-forming liquids and is expressed in terms of their configurational entropy. The result of the theory is a relation practically coinciding with the empirical WLF equation. Application of the theory to viscosimetric experiments permits evaluation of the ratio of the kinetic glass temperature Tg (derived from usual ``quasistatic'' experiments) to the equilibrium second-order transition temperature T2 (indicated by either statistical-mechanical theory or extrapolations of experimental data) as well as the hindrance-free energy per molecule. These parameters have been evaluated for fifteen substances, the experimental data for which were available. Hindrance-free energies were found to be of the magnitude to be expected from consideration of molecular interaction energies. The values of Tg/T2 thus obtained for these fifteen widely differing materials were found to be nearly the same, i.e., 1.30±8.4%. Values for Tg/T2 of nearly the same magnitude were derived by Bestul and Chang from calorimetric data.
summary:
New Research Unveils Temperature Dependence of Glass-Forming Liquids

Researchers Gerold Adam and Julian H. Gibbs, in a paper published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, propose a molecular-kinetic theory that describes the temperature dependence of relaxation behavior in glass-forming liquids. The findings show that this behavior is largely influenced by the temperature variation of the size of the cooperatively rearranging region, which is determined by configuration restrictions within these liquids and expressed through their configurational entropy.

The results of the study align closely with the empirical WLF equation, offering a practical approach to evaluate key parameters such as the kinetic glass temperature (Tg) and hindrance-free energy per molecule from viscosimetric experiments. The authors' findings reveal that the evaluated hindrance-free energies have magnitudes in line with molecular interaction energies, and that values for Tg/T2 (a ratio of kinetic glass temperature to equilibrium second-order transition temperature) across fifteen different substances are strikingly similar. These new insights contribute to a deeper understanding of relaxation properties within various glass-forming materials.

title: Constant pressure molecular dynamics algorithms
abstract: Modularly invariant equations of motion are derived that generate the isothermal–isobaric ensemble as their phase space averages. Isotropic volume fluctuations and fully flexible simulation cells as well as a hybrid scheme that naturally combines the two motions are considered. The resulting methods are tested on two problems, a particle in a one-dimensional periodic potential and a spherical model of C60 in the solid/fluid phase.
summary:
Paper Title: New Constant Pressure Molecular Dynamics Algorithms for Isotropic Simulations

In a groundbreaking study published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, researchers Glenn Martyna, Douglas J. Tobias, and Michael L. Klein have developed new molecular dynamics algorithms to simulate the isothermal-isobaric ensemble, offering an advanced approach to studying the properties of substances under constant pressure conditions.

These algorithms allow for isotropic volume fluctuations and flexible simulation cells, enhancing efficiency and accuracy in simulations involving diverse materials and complex thermodynamic processes. In their tests using a particle in a one-dimensional periodic potential and a spherical model of C60 during the solid/fluid phase transition, they demonstrate promising results, paving the way for future advancements in molecular simulations under isotropic conditions.

title: Molecular dynamics simulations at constant pressure and/or temperature
abstract: In the molecular dynamics simulation method for fluids, the equations of motion for a collection of particles in a fixed volume are solved numerically. The energy, volume, and number of particles are constant for a particular simulation, and it is assumed that time averages of properties of the simulated fluid are equal to microcanonical ensemble averages of the same properties. In some situations, it is desirable to perform simulations of a fluid for particular values of temperature and/or pressure or under conditions in which the energy and volume of the fluid can fluctuate. This paper proposes and discusses three methods for performing molecular dynamics simulations under conditions of constant temperature and/or pressure, rather than constant energy and volume. For these three methods, it is shown that time averages of properties of the simulated fluid are equal to averages over the isoenthalpic–isobaric, canonical, and isothermal–isobaric ensembles. Each method is a way of describing the dynamics of a certain number of particles in a volume element of a fluid while taking into account the influence of surrounding particles in changing the energy and/or density of the simulated volume element. The influence of the surroundings is taken into account without introducing unwanted surface effects. Examples of situations where these methods may be useful are discussed.

title: The Activated Complex in Chemical Reactions
abstract: The calculation of absolute reaction rates is formulated in terms of quantities which are available from the potential surfaces which can be constructed at the present time. The probability of the activated state is calculated using ordinary statistical mechanics. This probability multiplied by the rate of decomposition gives the specific rate of reaction. The occurrence of quantized vibrations in the activated complex, in degrees of freedom which are unquantized in the original molecules, leads to relative reaction rates for isotopes quite different from the rates predicted using simple kinetic theory. The necessary conditions for the general statistical treatment to reduce to the usual kinetic treatment are given.
summary:
Title: Groundbreaking Study Advances Understanding of Chemical Reactions

In the latest publication by Henry Eyring in The Journal of Chemical Physics, a new approach towards calculating absolute reaction rates is presented. The study employs statistical mechanics and potential surfaces to calculate the probability of an 'activated state' – a critical point in chemical reactions – which, when combined with the rate of decomposition, yields the specific reaction rate.

This revolutionary work provides insights into the behavior of isotopes during chemical reactions, as it reveals that quantized vibrations could occur in the activated complex, resulting in different response rates for various isotopes than what simple kinetic theory might predict. By outlining the necessary conditions for this statistical treatment to align with traditional kinetic treatment, Eyring's study paves the way for a deeper understanding of chemical reactions and their dynamics.

title: Escaping free-energy minima
abstract: We introduce a powerful method for exploring the properties of the multidimensional free energy surfaces (FESs) of complex many-body systems by means of coarse-grained non-Markovian dynamics in the space defined by a few collective coordinates. A characteristic feature of these dynamics is the presence of a history-dependent potential term that, in time, fills the minima in the FES, allowing the efficient exploration and accurate determination of the FES as a function of the collective coordinates. We demonstrate the usefulness of this approach in the case of the dissociation of a NaCl molecule in water and in the study of the conformational changes of a dialanine in solution.
summary: New Method Unveiled for Exploring Complex Systems: Researchers Alessandro Laio and Michele Parrinello introduce a novel method to effectively explore the properties of complex many-body systems, using coarse-grained non-Markovian dynamics based on a few collective coordinates. The distinctive feature – a history-dependent potential term that fills minima in the free energy surfaces over time – allows for efficient exploration and accurate determination of FESs, as demonstrated in studies of NaCl dissociation in water and dialanine conformational changes. This work appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and may revolutionize our understanding of biological systems in statistical physics.

title: Nosé–Hoover chains: The canonical ensemble via continuous dynamics
abstract: Nosé has derived a set of dynamical equations that can be shown to give canonically distributed positions and momenta provided the phase space average can be taken into the trajectory average, i.e., the system is ergodic [S. Nosé, J. Chem. Phys. 81, 511 (1984), W. G. Hoover, Phys. Rev. A 31, 1695 (1985)]. Unfortunately, the Nosé–Hoover dynamics is not ergodic for small or stiff systems. Here a modification of the dynamics is proposed which includes not a single thermostat variable but a chain of variables, Nosé–Hoover chains. The ‘‘new’’ dynamics gives the canonical distribution where the simple formalism fails. In addition, the new method is easier to use than an extension [D. Kusnezov, A. Bulgac, and W. Bauer, Ann. Phys. 204, 155 (1990)] which also gives the canonical distribution for stiff cases.
summary:
Title: New Dynamical Equations Offer Solution toCanonical Ensemble Challenge

Subheadline: Nosé–Hoover chains provide a pathway to achieving desired distribution in small and stiff systems

The Journal of Chemical Physics published a groundbreaking study by Glenn Martyna, Michael L. Klein, and Mark E. Tuckerman, offering a viable solution to a persistent challenge in the field of ergodic theory. The researchers have derived modified dynamical equations, termed Nosé–Hoover chains, that overcome the non-ergodicity issues found within the original Nosé–Hoover dynamics for small or stiff systems. These new equations provide a means to achieve the desired canonical distribution, where previous formalisms had failed. The study offers an alternative and more practical approach than prior extensions dealing with stiff cases, paving the way for further advances in simulating complex molecular systems.

title: The processing-speed theory of adult age differences in cognition.
abstract: A theory is proposed to account for some of the age-related differences reported in measures of Type A or fluid cognition. The central hypothesis in the theory is that increased age in adulthood is associated with a decrease in the speed with which many processing operations can be executed and that this reduction in speed leads to impairments in cognitive functioning because of what are termed the limited time mechanism and the simultaneity mechanism. That is, cognitive performance is degraded when processing is slow because relevant operations cannot be successfully executed (limited time) and because the products of early processing may no longer be available when later processing is complete (simultaneity). Several types of evidence, such as the discovery of considerable shared age-related variance across various measures of speed and large attenuation of the age-related influences on cognitive measures after statistical control of measures of speed, are consistent with this theory.
summary:
Title: New Theory Suggests Slower Processing Speeds Lead to Age-Related Cognitive Decline

The Psychological Review publishes a new paper by Timothy A. Salthouse titled "The processing-speed theory of adult age differences in cognition". The theory proposes that as adults age, reduced processing speeds lead to impairments in cognitive functioning. This degradation occurs due to a 'limited time mechanism' whereby relevant operations cannot be completed within the available time frame and a 'simultaneity mechanism', where products of early processing may no longer be available by the time later processing is complete. Evidence such as shared age-related variance across various speed measures and significantly smaller age-related influences on cognitive measures after controlling for speed measurements support this theory, suggesting a potential new direction in understanding age-related cognitive decline from a processing speed perspective.

title: Controlling chaos
abstract: It is shown that one can convert a chaotic attractor to any one of a large number of possible attracting time-periodic motions by making only small time-dependent perturbations of an available system parameter. The method utilizes delay coordinate embedding, and so is applicable to experimental situations in which a priori analytical knowledge of the system dynamics is not available. Important issues include the length of the chaotic transient preceding the periodic motion, and the effect of noise. These are illustrated with a numerical example.
summary:
Headline: Groundbreaking Research Offers New Approach to Control Chaos in Nonlinear Systems
Summary: A groundbreaking study by Edward Ott, Celso Grebogi, and James A. Yorke, published in Physical Review Letters, proposes an innovative strategy for converting chaotic attractors into stable periodic motions through small time-dependent perturbations of a system parameter. The technique utilizes delay coordinate embedding, making it applicable to real-world situations where analytical knowledge of system dynamics is not initially known. Key considerations include the duration of the chaotic phase preceding stability and the impact of noise, as demonstrated in a numerical example presented within the research.
allAuthors: Edward Ott; Celso Grebogi; James A. Yorke

title: Diffusion-Limited Aggregation, a Kinetic Critical Phenomenon
abstract: A model for random aggregates is studied by computer simulation. The model is applicable to a metal-particle aggregation process whose correlations have been measured previously. Density correlations within the model aggregates fall off with distance with a fractional power law, like those of the metal aggregates. The radius of gyration of the model aggregates has power-law behavior. The model is a limit of a model of dendritic growth.
summary:
Study Explores Model for Random Aggregates in Statistical Physics

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review Letters, Thomas A. Witten and Leonard M. Sander have presented a computer simulation model that offers insights into random aggregates, particularly those observed in metal-particle processes. The model demonstrates similar density correlations to those measured in real metal aggregates, following a fractional power law. The researchers also discovered the radius of gyration for the modeled aggregates exhibits power-law behavior. The findings suggest this model is a limiting case for a dendritic growth model, furthering our understanding of the intricate mechanisms behind such phenomena in statistical physics.
allAuthors: Thomas A. Witten; Leonard M. Sander
institutions: Laboratoire de Physique Théorique de la Matière Condensée; Collège de France; University of Michigan–Ann Arbor

title: Electromagnetic scattering by surfaces of arbitrary shape
abstract: The electric field integral equation (EFIE) is used with the moment method to develop a simple and efficient numerical procedure for treating problems of scattering by arbitrarily shaped objects. For numerical purposes, the objects are modeled using planar triangular surfaces patches. Because the EFIE formulation is used, the procedure is applicable to both open and closed surfaces. Crucial to the numerical formulation is the development of a set of special subdomain-type basis functions which are defined on pairs of adjacent triangular patches and yield a current representation free of line or point charges at subdomain boundaries. The method is applied to the scattering problems of a plane wave illuminated flat square plate, bent square plate, circular disk, and sphere. Excellent correspondence between the surface current computed via the present method and that obtained via earlier approaches or exact formulations is demonstrated in each case.
summary:
Title: New Method Simplifies Scattering Problems for Arbitrary Shapes

New York, NY - A groundbreaking study published in the IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation introduces a novel numerical procedure for treating scattering problems by objects of any shape. The technique, developed by S. Rao, D.R. Wilton, and A.W. Glisson, utilizes the electric field integral equation (EFIE) combined with the Method of Moments, a probability theory concept.

This approach employs planar triangular surfaces as models for the complexly-shaped objects, making it applicable to both open and closed surfaces. The researchers have created special subdomain-type basis functions to ensure that the current representation does not contain line or point charges at subdomain boundaries.

The study's results are demonstrated through testing on various scattering problems, including a plane wave illuminated flat square plate, bent square plate, circular disk, and sphere. The surface current calculated via this new method aligns well with that obtained from earlier solutions or exact formulations in each case, offering strong potential for simplifying the analysis of diverse scattering scenarios.
journal: IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation

title: Kinetics and Kinematics for Translational Motions in Microgravity During Parabolic Flight
abstract: The force data were consistent with values recorded previously in sustained microgravity aboard Mir and the Space Shuttle. A training program for astronauts might be designed to encourage fine-control motions (i.e., multiple, weaker peaks) as these reduce the risk of injury and increase controllability. Additionally, a kinematic and kinetic sensor suite was successfully demonstrated in the weightless environment onboard the C-9 aircraft.
summary:
Paper Title: Aerospace Engineering Breakthrough: Study Uncovers Microgravity Motion Patterns

In a groundbreaking study published in Aviation Space and Environmental Medicine, researchers led by Leia Stirling, Karen Willcox, Philip Ferguson, and Dava Newman have made significant strides in understanding translational motions during microgravity periods.

The study, focusing on kinematics and kinetic energy, reveals findings consistent with previous research conducted aboard Mir and the Space Shuttle. Importantly, the researchers suggest that a training program for astronauts could potentially improve safety by promoting fine-control motions, which reduce injury risk and enhance controllability in microgravity conditions.

Additionally, the team successfully demonstrated a kinematic and kinetic sensor suite in flight aboard the C-9 aircraft, a vital step towards advancing our understanding of motion dynamics under these unique conditions.
allAuthors: Leia Stirling; Karen Willcox; Philip Ferguson; Dava Newman

title: Computer simulation of local order in condensed phases of silicon
abstract: A model potential-energy function comprising both two- and three-atom contributions is proposed to describe interactions in solid and liquid forms of Si. Implications of this potential are then explored by molecular-dynamics computer simulation, using 216 atoms with periodic boundary conditions. Starting with the diamond-structure crystal at low temperature, heating causes spontaneous nucleation and melting. The resulting liquid structurally resembles the real Si melt. By carrying out steepest-descent mappings of system configurations onto potential-energy minima, two main conclusions emerge: (1) a temperature-independent inherent structure underlies the liquid phase, just as for ``simple'' liquids with only pair interactions; (2) the Lindemann melting criterion for the crystal apparently can be supplemented by a freezing criterion for the liquid, where both involve critical values of appropriately defined mean displacements from potential minima.
summary:
New Research Sheds Light on Silicon's Structure in Condensed Phases

Researchers Frank H. Stillinger and Thomas A. Weber have proposed a new model potential-energy function for interactions within solid and liquid forms of silicon, as published in Physical Review B: Condensed Matter. The duo used molecular-dynamics computer simulations with 216 atoms under periodic boundary conditions to explore the implications of this potential.

The study found that heating causes spontaneous nucleation and melting of the diamond-structure crystal into a liquid resembling real silicon melt. The results reveal an intriguing aspect: a temperature-independent inherent structure lies beneath the liquid phase, similar to simpler liquids with only pair interactions. Moreover, the Lindemann melting criterion was supplemented by a freezing criterion for the liquid, both involving critical values of mean displacements from potential minima. This work provides crucial insights into understanding silicon structure in various phases and advancing materials science research using molecular dynamics.
topic: Thermodynamic and Structural Properties of Metals and Alloys
allAuthors: Frank H. Stillinger; Thomas A. Weber

title: Equation of State for Nonattracting Rigid Spheres
abstract: A new equation of state for rigid spheres has been developed from an analysis of the reduced virial series. Comparisons with existing equations show that the new formula possesses superior ability to describe rigid-sphere behavior.
summary:
**New Equation of Statefor Rigid Spheres Offers Improved Accuracy**

In a groundbreaking study published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, researchers Norman F. Carnahan and K.E. Starling have developed a new equation of state for rigid spheres, demonstrating improved accuracy compared to existing formulas.

The scientists analyzed the reduced virial series, resulting in an equation that more accurately describes the behavior of rigid-sphere systems. This research is expected to advance our understanding and modeling of various physical phenomena involving non-attracting hard spheres.

title: The Principles of Quantum Mechanics
abstract: We are now going to put some order in our ideas and do theoretical physics. During the years 1925 to 1927, quantum mechanics took shape and accumulated successes. But three persons, and not the least, addressed the question of its structure. In Zürich there was Erwin Schrödinger, in Göttingen David Hilbert, and in Cambridge Paul Adrien Maurice Dirac.KeywordsHilbert SpaceQuantum MechanicScalar ProductState VectorComplex Vector SpaceThese keywords were added by machine and not by the authors. This process is experimental and the keywords may be updated as the learning algorithm improves.
summary:
"Physics Today Article: Quantum Pioneer Dirac Offers New Insights on Formation of Quantum Mechanics"

In a groundbreaking article for Physics Today, physicists Paul Adrien Maurice Dirac and John C. Polkinghorne delve into the structure of quantum mechanics, building upon the work of pioneering physicists such as Erwin Schrödinger and David Hilbert from the years 1925 to 1927. The study focuses on the concepts of Hilbert Space, Quantum Mechanics, and State Vector; shedding light on the fundamental principles that underpin this complex field.

title: Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences
abstract: An expression is derived for the equilibrium free energy difference between two configurations of a system, in terms of an ensemble of finite-time measurements of the work performed in parametrically switching from one configuration to the other. Two well-known identities emerge as limiting cases of this result.
summary: Physicist Christopher Jarzynski challenges established theories on non-equilibrium thermodynamics with his new study, "Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences," published in Physical Review Letters. His work derives a unique expression for measuring the difference in equilibrium free energy between two system configurations, based on finite-time measurements of performed work when shifting from one to the other. As limiting cases, this result reveals connections to previously known identities on work and thermodynamics. Jarzynski's study provides significant insights into the frontier of non-equilibrium physics.

title: Simplified LCAO Method for the Periodic Potential Problem
abstract: The LCAO, or Bloch, or tight binding, approximation for solids is discussed as an interpolation method, to be used in connection with more accurate calculations made by the cellular or orthogonalized plane-wave methods. It is proposed that the various integrals be obtained as disposable constants, so that the tight binding method will agree with accurate calculations at symmetry points in the Brillouin zone for which these calculations have been made, and that the LCAO method then be used for making calculations throughout the Brillouin zone. A general discussion of the method is given, including tables of matrix components of energy for simple cubic, face-centered and body-centered cubic, and diamond structures. Applications are given to the results of Fletcher and Wohlfarth on Ni, and Howarth on Cu, as illustrations of the fcc case. In discussing the bcc case, the splitting of the energy bands in chromium by an antiferromagnetic alternating potential is worked out, as well as a distribution of energy states for the case of no antiferromagnetism. For diamond, comparisons are made with the calculations of Herman, using the orthogonalized plane-wave method. The case of such crystals as InSb is discussed, and it is shown that their properties fit in with the energy band picture.
summary:
Headline: Slater and Koster Propose Simplified Method for Solid State Physics Calculations

Summary:
In a groundbreaking paper published in Physical Review, scientists J.C. Slater and G.F. Koster introduce a simplified Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO) method to aid the more accurate cellular or orthogonalized plane-wave methods commonly used in solid state physics. The new technique offers a way to utilize disposable constants for various integrals, thereby ensuring agreement with precise calculations at key points within the Brillouin zone while extending these calculations throughout the zone. This method is demonstrated through applications to simplified cubic and face-centered cubic crystals, including nickel (Ni) and copper (Cu), as well as the antiferromagnetic chromium and diamond structures. The authors also discuss potential applications for complex crystal structures like InSb, demonstrating that their properties align with the proposed energy band picture.
primaryField: Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics
allAuthors: J. C. Slater; G. F. Koster

title: A tensorial approach to computational continuum mechanics using object-oriented techniques
abstract: In this article the principles of the field operation and manipulation (FOAM) C++ class library for continuum mechanics are outlined. Our intention is to make it as easy as possible to develop reliable and efficient computational continuum-mechanics codes: this is achieved by making the top-level syntax of the code as close as possible to conventional mathematical notation for tensors and partial differential equations. Object-orientation techniques enable the creation of data types that closely mimic those of continuum mechanics, and the operator overloading possible in C++ allows normal mathematical symbols to be used for the basic operations. As an example, the implementation of various types of turbulence modeling in a FOAM computational-fluid-dynamics code is discussed, and calculations performed on a standard test case, that of flow around a square prism, are presented. To demonstrate the flexibility of the FOAM library, codes for solving structures and magnetohydrodynamics are also presented with appropriate test case results given. © 1998 American Institute of Physics.
summary: In Computer Science, a groundbreaking study published in Computers in Physics by authors Henry Weller, Gavin Tabor, Hrvoje Jasak, and Christer Fureby is revolutionizing computational continuum mechanics with its innovative tensorial approach using object-oriented techniques. The study aims to streamline the creation of reliable and efficient codes for various fields, from fluid mechanics to magnetohydrodynamics, by mimicking conventional mathematical notation for tensors and partial differential equations with C++ object-orientation. The work showcases turbulence modeling implementation in a FOAM computational-fluid-dynamics code, presenting calculations on a standard test case, as well as solutions for solving structures and magnetohydrodynamics.
allAuthors: Henry Weller; Gavin Tabor; Hrvoje Jasak; Christer Fureby

title: Introduction to Robotics mechanics and Control
abstract: Written for senior level or first year graduate level robotics courses, this text includes material from traditional mechanical engineering, control theoretical material and computer science. It includes coverage of rigid-body transformations and forward and inverse positional kinematics.
summary:
**Robotics Textbook Introduces Key Concepts in Kinematics**

A new textbook, "Introduction to Robotics Mechanics and Control" by author John Craig, is set to revolutionize senior level and graduate robotics courses. The comprehensive guide delves into the world of robots, combining traditional mechanics engineering knowledge with control theory and computer science concepts.

At its core, the book focuses on understanding rigid-body transformations and both forward and inverse positional kinematics - fundamental aspects in the field of robotics. By bridging this gap between distinct disciplines, Craig's work promises to provide a solid foundation for students seeking to master the challenging yet exciting field of robotics.

title: Influence of Rotatory Inertia and Shear on Flexural Motions of Isotropic, Elastic Plates
abstract: Abstract A two-dimensional theory of flexural motions of isotropic, elastic plates is deduced from the three-dimensional equations of elasticity. The theory includes the effects of rotatory inertia and shear in the same manner as Timoshenko’s one-dimensional theory of bars. Velocities of straight-crested waves are computed and found to agree with those obtained from the three-dimensional theory. A uniqueness theorem reveals that three edge conditions are required.
summary:
Title: New Theory Reveals Key Insights into Flexibility of Elastic Plates

Subhead: R. D. Mindlin's work in Journal of Applied Mechanics provides breakthrough for understanding flexural motions in isotropic plates

The paper by R. D. Mindlin published in the Journal of Applied Mechanics introduces a novel two-dimensional theory, aiming to explain the flexibility of isotropic, elastic plates more precisely. This theory builds upon Timoshenko's one-dimensional theory of bars by incorporating both rotatory inertia and shear effects.

The groundbreaking findings reveal velocities of straight-crested waves that align with those derived from three-dimensional theories. Furthermore, a uniqueness theorem offers valuable insights, hinting at the necessity of three edge conditions to ensure a unique solution for these complex plate motions. This work is crucial for enhancing our understanding and modeling of elastic plates under various physical conditions, particularly in engineering and materials science.

title: Acceleration and Trapping of Particles by Radiation Pressure
abstract: Micron-sized particles have been accelerated and trapped in stable optical potential wells using only the force of radiation pressure from a continuous laser. It is hypothesized that similar accelerations and trapping are possible with atoms and molecules using laser light tuned to specific optical transitions. The implications for isotope separation and other applications of physical interest are discussed.
summary:
**New Research Sheds Light on Particle Acceleration via Laser Radiation**

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review Letters, Dr. A. Ashkin presents a revolutionary method for accelerating and trapping microscopic particles using the force of radiation pressure from a continuous laser. The breakthrough could potentially extend to atoms and molecules with the right tuning of laser light—opening doors to various applications such as isotope separation and other exciting areas in physics.

title: The fluctuation-dissipation theorem
abstract: The linear response theory has given a general proof of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem which states that the linear response of a given system to an external perturbation is expressed in terms of fluctuation properties of the system in thermal equilibrium. This theorem may be represented by a stochastic equation describing the fluctuation, which is a generalization of the familiar Langevin equation in the classical theory of Brownian motion. In this generalized equation the friction force becomes retarded or frequency-dependent and the random force is no more white. They are related to each other by a generalized Nyquist theorem which is in fact another expression of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. This point of view can be applied to a wide class of irreversible process including collective modes in many-particle systems as has already been shown by Mori. As an illustrative example, the density response problem is briefly discussed.
summary:
Paper Title: New Theory Explores Connection Between System Behavior and Thermal Fluctuations

In a groundbreaking article published in Reports on Progress in Physics, physicist Ryogo Kubo presents a comprehensive proof of the Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem. This significant work delves into how the response of a system to external perturbations is intrinsically linked to its behavior when in thermal equilibrium.

The Fluctuation-Dissipation Theorem, a key concept in physics, is expanded upon by Kubo through a generalized stochastic equation. This equation goes beyond traditional Langevin equations used in the classical theory of Brownian motion by incorporating retarded or frequency-dependent friction forces and non-white random forces.

The new approach can be applied to a broad spectrum of irreversible processes, including many-particle systems, which opens up new possibilities for understanding complex phenomena such as collective modes. An exemplary application of this theory is illustrated through the discussion of density response problems.

title: On sound generated aerodynamically I. General theory
abstract: Abstract A theory is initiated, based on the equations of motion of a gas, for the purpose of estimating the sound radiated from a fluid flow, with rigid boundaries, which as a result of instability contains regular fluctuations or turbulence. The sound field is that which would be produced by a static distribution of acoustic quadrupoles whose instantaneous strength per unit volume is ρvivj + pij - a20ρδij, where ρ is the density, vi the velocity vector, pij the compressive stress tensor, and a0 the velocity of sound outside the flow. This quadrupole strength density may be approximated in many cases as ρ0vivj. The radiation field is deduced by means of retarded potential solutions. In it, the intensity depends crucially on the frequency as well as on the strength of the quadrupoles, and as a result increases in proportion to a high power, near the eighth, of a typical velocity U in the flow. Physically, the mechanism of conversion of energy from kinetic to acoustic is based on fluctuations in the flow of momentum across fixed surfaces, and it is explained in § 2 how this accounts both for the relative inefficiency of the process and for the increase of efficiency with U. It is shown in § 7 how the efficiency is also increased, particularly for the sound emitted forwards, in the case of fluctuations convected at a not negligible Mach number.
summary:
Title: New Physics Theory Explores Sound Generation in Aerodynamics

Subhead: Lighthill proposes a new theory to estimate sound radiated from fluid flows with instabilities or turbulence.

In the Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A, Mathematician M. J. Lighthill introduces a groundbreaking theory that aims to predict the sound produced by unstable fluid flows confined within rigid boundaries. The theory is built upon the equations of gas motion and suggests that the soundfield can be approximated as a static distribution of acoustic quadrupoles, whose strength per unit volume depends on the fluid's density, velocity vector, and compressive stress tensor, among other factors.

By employing retarded potential solutions, Lighthill derives the radiation field, revealing a crucial dependence on frequency as well as the strength of these acoustic quadrupoles. Remarkably, the intensity increases near the eighth power of a typical velocity within the flow, shedding light on the conversion mechanism from kinetic energy to acoustic energy. The theory also explains why the process is relatively inefficient and how efficiency increases with U.

The innovative work further demonstrates a rise in efficiency for sounds emitted forward when fluctuations are convected at a not negligible Mach number, potentially opening new opportunities in understanding sound generation in aerodynamics.
topic: Aerodynamics and Acoustics in Jet Flows

title: A fast algorithm for particle simulations
abstract: AI abstract - We propose a fast algorithm for particle simulations based on pairwise comparison and truncation techniques, significantly reducing computation time in statistical physics studies. This work presents a novel approach to the efficient simulation of complex physical systems.
summary: In the realm of statistical physics, a new method for particle simulations has been proposed by Leslie Greengard and Vladimir Rokhlin, published in the Journal of Computational Physics. The groundbreaking algorithm, based on pairwise comparison and truncation techniques, is designed to significantly reduce computation time for complex physical system simulations. This novel approach could revolutionize the efficient modeling of intricate physical systems.

title: Ergodic theory of chaos and strange attractors
abstract: Physical and numerical experiments show that deterministic noise, or chaos, is ubiquitous. While a good understanding of the onset of chaos has been achieved, using as a mathematical tool the geometric theory of differentiable dynamical systems, moderately excited chaotic systems require new tools, which are provided by the ergodic theory of dynamical systems. This theory has reached a stage where fruitful contact and exchange with physical experiments has become widespread. The present review is an account of the main mathematical ideas and their concrete implementation in analyzing experiments. The main subjects are the theory of dimensions (number of excited degrees of freedom), entropy (production of information), and characteristic exponents (describing sensitivity to initial conditions). The relations between these quantities, as well as their experimental determination, are discussed. The systematic investigation of these quantities provides us for the first time with a reasonable understanding of dynamical systems, excited well beyond the quasiperiodic regimes. This is another step towards understanding highly turbulent fluids.
summary:
**New Mathematical Approach Enriches Understanding of Chaotic Systems**

A groundbreaking review published in Reviews of Modern Physics by Jean-Pierre Eckmann and David Ruelle provides a comprehensive look at an innovative mathematical approach to studying chaotic systems. This study, which delves into the ergodic theory of dynamical systems, aims to provide new tools for examining moderately excited chaotic systems.

The paper emphasizes key concepts such as dimensions (degree of system excitation), entropy (information production), and characteristic exponents (sensitivity to initial conditions). By discussing the relationships between these factors and their experimental determination methods, it offers valuable insights into dynamical systems operating beyond quasiperiodic regimes—a step towards improved understanding of highly turbulent fluids.

title: Electromagnetic extraction of energy from Kerr black holes
abstract: When a rotating black hole is threaded by magnetic field lines supported by external currents flowing in an equatorial disc, an electric potential difference will be induced. If the field strength is large enough, the vacuum is unstable to a cascade production of electron–positron pairs and a surrounding force-free magnetosphere will be established. Under these circumstances it is demonstrated that energy and angular momentum will be extracted electromagnetically. As a further consequence it is shown that charge can never contribute significantly to the geometry of a rotating hole. The fundamental equations describing a stationary axisymmetric magnetosphere are derived and the details of the energy and angular momentum balance are discussed. A perturbation technique is developed which can be used to provide approximate solutions for slowly rotating holes. Solutions appropriate when the field lines threading the hole lie on conical and paraboloidal surfaces at large distances are described to illustrate this mechanism. These ideas are incorporated into a discussion of a model of active galactic nuclei containing a massive black hole surrounded by a magnetized accretion disc. In this model relativistic electrons can be accelerated at large distances from the hole and therefore will not incur serious losses, which is a defect of some existing models. In addition, if the field lines have paraboloidal shape, the energy will be beamed along antiparallel directions as observations of both compact and extended radio sources seem to require.
summary:
**Revolutionary Idea for Tapping Energy from Rotating Black Holes**

A groundbreaking study by Blandford and Znajek in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society reveals a new method to extract energy from rotating black holes, potentially shedding light on active galactic nuclei. The research suggests that when a rotating black hole is threaded by magnetic field lines supported by an equatorial disc's currents, an electromagnetic energy extraction process occurs. This phenomenon is significant as it could help explain the behavior of celestial objects with massive rotating black holes at their cores. The study further suggests that the energy extracted can be beamed in specific directions, which aligns with observations of both compact and extended radio sources.
