New Study Provides Insights on Geophysical Fluid Dynamics

In the Journal of Applied Mechanics, researchers Joseph Pedlosky and S. Leibovich delve into the complex world of inviscid flow, presenting a groundbreaking study on geophysical fluid dynamics. This new research builds upon prior work exploring friction and viscous flow in the oceanic circulation, shedding light on the instability theory that governs ageostrophic motion in a stratified fluid on a sphere. The findings aim to offer valuable insights into the mechanics of geology and the wind-driven oceanic patterns that shape our environment.

title: Notes on black-hole evaporation
abstract: This paper examines various aspects of black-hole evaporation. A two-dimensional model is investigated where it is shown that using fermion-boson cancellation on the stress-energy tensor reduces the energy outflow to zero, while other noncovariant techniques give the Hawking result. A technique for replacing the collapse by boundary conditions on the past horizon is developed which retains the essential features of the collapse while eliminating some of the difficulties. This set of boundary conditions is also suggested as the most natural set for a preexistent black hole. The behavior of particle detectors under acceleration is investigated where it is shown that an accelerated detector even in flat spacetime will detect particles in the vacuum. The similarity of this case with the behavior of a detector near the black hole is brought out, and it is shown that a geodesic detector near the horizon will not see the Hawking flux of particles. Finally, the work of Berger, Chitre, Nutku, and Moncrief on scalar geons is corrected, and the spherically symmetric coupled scalar-gravitation Hamiltonian is presented in the hope that someone can apply it to the problem of black-hole evaporation.
summary:
Headline: "New Study Questions Black Hole Evaporation Rates, Suggests Revised Model"

Summary:
In a new paper published in Physical Review, physicist W.G. Unruh challenges the traditional understanding of black hole evaporation. By employing a two-dimensional model and fermion-boson cancellation on the stress-energy tensor, Unruh reduces the energy outflow to zero, contrasting with other noncovariant techniques that align with the Hawking result. The researcher also develops a set of boundary conditions for a preexistent black hole and investigates the behavior of particle detectors under acceleration, demonstrating parallels between this case and the behavior of a detector near a black hole. Interestingly, Unruh's findings suggest that a geodesic detector near the horizon will not perceive the Hawking flux of particles. Lastly, the study aims to correct previous work on scalar geons and presents a spherically symmetric coupled scalar-gravitation Hamiltonian towards addressing black hole evaporation issues further.

title: On differential equations of nonlocal elasticity and solutions of screw dislocation and surface waves
abstract: Integropartial differential equations of the linear theory of nonlocal elasticity are reduced to singular partial differential equations for a special class of physically admissible kernels. Solutions are obtained for the screw dislocation and surface waves. Experimental observations and atomic lattice dynamics appear to support the theoretical results very nicely.
summary:
In Breakthrough Study, Physicist A. Cemal Eringen Uncovers Key Insights into Nonlocal Elasticity

The journal of Applied Physics has published a groundbreaking paper by physicist Dr. A. Cemal Eringen, reducing complex integropartial differential equations in the linear theory of nonlocal elasticity to simpler singular partial differential equations for certain physically viable kernels. The study offers practical solutions for the screw dislocation and surface waves, findings that align well with experimental observations and atomic lattice dynamics. This work is set to significantly advance our understanding of elasticity, bringing us a step closer to deciphering the intricate mechanics at play in condensed matter physics.

Title: New Research Advances Understanding of Quantum Behavior in Electron Systems

title: On kinematic waves II. A theory of traffic flow on long crowded roads
abstract: Abstract This paper uses the method of kinematic waves, developed in part I, but may be read independently. A functional relationship between flow and concentration for traffic on crowded arterial roads has been postulated for some time, and has experimental backing (§2). From this a theory of the propagation of changes in traffic distribution along these roads may be deduced (§§2, 3). The theory is applied (§4) to the problem of estimating how a ‘hump’, or region of increased concentration, will move along a crowded main road. It is suggested that it will move slightly slower than the mean vehicle speed, and that vehicles passing through it will have to reduce speed rather suddenly (at a ‘shock wave’) on entering it, but can increase speed again only very gradually as they leave it. The hump gradually spreads out along the road, and the time scale of this process is estimated. The behaviour of such a hump on entering a bottleneck, which is too narrow to admit the increased flow, is studied (§5), and methods are obtained for estimating the extent and duration of the resulting hold-up. The theory is applicable principally to traffic behaviour over a long stretch of road, but the paper concludes (§6) with a discussion of its relevance to problems of flow near junctions, including a discussion of the starting flow at a controlled junction. In the introductory sections 1 and 2, we have included some elementary material on the quantitative study of traffic flow for the benefit of scientific readers unfamiliar with the subject.
summary:
Title: New Theory Predicts Traffic Flow on Congested Roads: "On kinematic waves II" Offers Insights

In the latest research paper published in Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A Mathematical and Physical Sciences, scientists M. J. Lighthill and G. B. Whitham have developed a theory to predict traffic flow on long, crowded roads using kinematic waves. This study builds upon previous work suggesting a functional relationship between traffic flow and concentration on arterial roads with experimental support (section 2).

The newly proposed theory deduces the propagation of changes in traffic distribution along these roads and offers insights into how so-called 'humps', or regions of increased concentration, will move along crowded main roads. According to the study, humps will move slightly slower than the mean vehicle speed and require vehicles passing through them to reduce speed abruptly upon entry (a "shock wave"). These vehicles can increase their speed gradually only as they leave the hump.

The researchers also investigate how a hump behaves when encountered by a bottleneck, which is too narrow to accommodate the increased flow. They provide methods for estimating the extent and duration of resulting hold-ups (section 5). Finally, the paper discusses the relevance of this research for traffic flow near junctions, including a discussion of starting flow at controlled junctions (section 6).
journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A Mathematical and Physical Sciences
allAuthors: M. J. Lighthill; G. B. Whitham

title: Transport, Collective Motion, and Brownian Motion
abstract: A theory of many-particle systems is developed to formulate transport, collective motion, and Brownian motion from a unified, statistical-mechanical point of view. This is done by, first, rewriting the equation of motion in a generalized form of the Langevin equation in the stochastic theory of Brownian motion and then, either studying the average evolution of a non-equilibrium system or calculating the linear response function to a mechanical perturbation. (1) An expression is obtained for the damping function φ(t), the real part of whose Laplace transform gives the damping constnat of collective motion. (2) A general equation of motion for a set of dynamical variables At) is derived, which takes the form where is a frequency matrix determining the collective oscillation of A(t). The quantity f(t) consists of those terms which are either non-linear in A(s), t ≧s ≧0, or dependent on the other degrees-of-freedom explicitly, and its time-correlation function is connected with the damping function φ(t) by (f(t1), f(t2)*) = φ(t1 − t2)·(A, A*). (3) An expression is obtained for the linear after-effect function to thermal disturbances such as temperature gradient and strain tensor. Both the conjugate fluxes and the time dependence differ from those of the mechanical response function. The conjugate fluxes are random parts of the fluxes of the state variables, thus depending on temperature. (4) The difference in the time dependence arises from a special property of the time evolution of f(t) and ensures that the damping function and the thermal after-effect function are determined by the microscopic processes in strong contrast to the mechanical response function. The difficulty of the plateau value problem in the previous theories of Brownian motion and transport coefficients is thus removed. (5) The theory is illustrated by dealing with the motion of inhomogeneous magnetization in ferromagnets and the Brownian motion of the collective coordinates of fluids. (6) Explicit expressions are derived for the thermal after-effect functions and the transport coefficients of multi-component systems.
summary:
Title: Unified Approach for Transport Phenomena Challenges Classical Physics Theories

In a groundbreaking scientific paper published in Progress of Theoretical Physics, Japanese physicist Hazime Mori presents a novel theory that reconciles transport, collective motion, and Brownian motion through a unified perspective based on statistical mechanics. The new approach addresses longstanding issues with prior theories concerning transport coefficients, particularly the "plateau value problem" (Brownian motion and transport phenomena).

The research builds upon the Langevin equation from stochastic theory of Brownian motion to provide an expression for the damping function associated with collective motion. Additionally, it derives a general equation of motion for dynamical variables that captures the effects of non-linear interactions and dependencies on other degrees-of-freedom (classical mechanics).

By examining the mechanical response to perturbations and thermal disturbances like temperature gradient and strain tensor, Mori's theory provides explicit expressions for the linear after-effect functions and transport coefficients in multi-component systems, surpassing earlier theories that had faced challenges regarding the time dependence of properties such as these.

Drawing upon earlier work by Millionshtchikov (1939), Kolmogorov proposes the components of velocity at any given point in a four-dimensional space to be treated as random variables. He assumes these velocities are finite and bounded within any confined subdomain, marking a notable departure from traditional approaches to turbulence studies.

The study aimed to support theories regarding the relationship between the scales of motions in highly turbulent flows, advancing our understanding of this complex and crucial aspect of fluid dynamics.

title: Constant pressure molecular dynamics simulation: The Langevin piston method
abstract: A new method for performing molecular dynamics simulations under constant pressure is presented. In the method, which is based on the extended system formalism introduced by Andersen, the deterministic equations of motion for the piston degree of freedom are replaced by a Langevin equation; a suitable choice of collision frequency then eliminates the unphysical ‘‘ringing’’ of the volume associated with the piston mass. In this way it is similar to the ‘‘weak coupling algorithm’’ developed by Berendsen and co-workers to perform molecular dynamics simulation without piston mass effects. It is shown, however, that the weak coupling algorithm induces artifacts into the simulation which can be quite severe for inhomogeneous systems such as aqueous biopolymers or liquid/liquid interfaces.
summary:
Title: New Method Enhances Constant Pressure Simulations for Complex Systems

In an innovative contribution to molecular dynamics, a team of researchers led by Scott E. Feller have presented a novel method that significantly improves simulations under constant pressure. This new approach, published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, seeks to address the "ringing" issue associated with conventional methods by replacing deterministic equations with a Langevin equation.

By implementing this approach, the team aims to eliminate unphysical oscillations in the volume while maintaining the accuracy of molecular dynamics simulations, much like the 'weak coupling algorithm' developed by Berendsen and colleagues. However, unlike previous methodologies, their new technique promises to provide more reliable results for complex systems such as aqueous biopolymers or liquid/liquid interfaces, which are prone to severe artifacts in traditional simulations.

title: A Kinematic Notation for Lower-Pair Mechanisms Based on Matrices
abstract: Abstract A symbolic notation devised by Reuleaux to describe mechanisms did not recognize the necessary number of variables needed for complete description. A reconsideration of the problem leads to a symbolic notation which permits the complete description of the kinematic properties of all lower-pair mechanisms by means of equations. The symbolic notation also yields a method for studying lower-pair mechanisms by means of matrix algebra; two examples of application to space mechanisms are given.
summary:
Paper Title: New Kinematic Notation for Mechanisms Simplifies Complex Calculations

In the Journal of Applied Mechanics, Denavit and Hartenberg propose a groundbreaking mathematical notation system for lower-pair mechanisms. This new system, built upon the prior work by Reuleaux, addresses earlier limitations in his symbolic notation by incorporating additional variables for complete descriptions of kinematic properties. The innovative approach allows for analysis through matrix algebra, streamlining complex calculations in the field of mechanism design, as demonstrated by two examples applied to space mechanisms.

title: Necessary and sufficient elastic stability conditions in various crystal systems
abstract: While the Born elastic stability criteria are well known for cubic crystals, there is some confusion in the literature about the form they should take for lower-symmetry crystal classes. Here we present closed form necessary and sufficient conditions for elastic stability in all crystal classes, as a concise and pedagogical reference to stability criteria in noncubic materials.
summary:
Title: New Elastic Stability Conditions Offered for Various Crystal Structures

In the realm of crystal physics, confusion has long clouded the literature regarding the elastic stability criteria beyond cubic crystals. Now, researchers Félix Mouhat and François‐Xavier Coudert, published in Physical Review B, aim to provide clarity with their new findings. The duo offers closed-form necessary and sufficient conditions for elastic stability in all crystal classes, offering a concise and accessible reference for stability criteria in noncubic materials. This work hopes to streamline the understanding of elastic stability in various crystal structures, providing insight into the world of materials science and the broader field of symmetry and learning theory.

title: Topology of cosmic domains and strings
abstract: The possible domain structures which can arise in the universe in a spontaneously broken gauge theory are studied. It is shown that the formation of domain wall, strings or monopoles depends on the homotopy groups of the manifold of degenerate vacua. The subsequent evolution of these structures is investigated. It is argued that while theories generating domain walls can probably be eliminated (because of their unacceptable gravitational effects), a cosmic network of strings may well have been formed and may have had important cosmological effects.
summary:
**New Study Provides Insight into the Formation of Cosmic Strings**

In a new paper published in the Journal of Physics A Mathematical and General, British physicist T. W. B. Kibble offers fresh insights on the potential domain structures that could have appeared in the universe, focusing on a theoretical framework called spontaneously broken gauge theory.

By examining the connection between homotopy groups of a manifold of degenerate vacua and the formation of specific structures such as domain walls, strings, or monopoles, Kibble's study sheds light on potential cosmic scenarios that could explain the presence of cosmic strings.

While theories involving domain walls are suggested to be unlikely due to their potentially disruptive gravitational effects, this research offers an intriguing perspective on a possible cosmic network of strings and their significant contributions to our cosmological understanding.
journal: Journal of Physics A Mathematical and General

title: Unity of All Elementary-Particle Forces
abstract: Strong, electromagnetic, and weak forces are conjectured to arise from a single fundamental interaction based on the gauge group SU(5).Received 10 January 1974DOI:https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.32.438©1974 American Physical Society

Headline: Fundamental Physics Theory Unites Three Essential Forces

A groundbreaking theory proposed by physicists Howard Georgi and Sheldon L. Glashow suggests that the strong, electromagnetic, and weak forces governing the behavior of elementary particles may stem from a single, unified fundamental interaction. Drawing upon the gauge group SU(5), their work, published in Physical Review Letters, aspires to consolidate disparate forces within the realm of physics and potentially simplify our understanding of the universe's basic building blocks.

title: The immersed boundary method
abstract: This paper is concerned with the mathematical structure of the immersed boundary (IB) method, which is intended for the computer simulation of fluid–structure interaction, especially in biological fluid dynamics. The IB formulation of such problems, derived here from the principle of least action, involves both Eulerian and Lagrangian variables, linked by the Dirac delta function. Spatial discretization of the IB equations is based on a fixed Cartesian mesh for the Eulerian variables, and a moving curvilinear mesh for the Lagrangian variables. The two types of variables are linked by interaction equations that involve a smoothed approximation to the Dirac delta function. Eulerian/Lagrangian identities govern the transfer of data from one mesh to the other. Temporal discretization is by a second-order Runge–Kutta method. Current and future research directions are pointed out, and applications of the IB method are briefly discussed.
summary:
In the realm of computer simulations for fluid-structure interaction, particularly in biological settings, renowned mathematician Charles S. Peskin presents a groundbreaking paper in Acta Numerica. Titled "The immersed boundary method", this study focuses on a novel approach to connect Eulerian and Lagrangian variables using the Dirac delta function.

Building upon previous research about discretization, curvilinear coordinates, and smoothed Dirac delta functions, Peskin's work aims to structure the Immersed Boundary method mathematically for these types of simulations. The discreet representation of the immersed boundary equations employs a stationary Cartesian grid for Eulerian variables and a mobile curvilinear grid for Lagrangian variables, linked by interaction equations involving smoothed versions of the Dirac delta function.

The paper also proposes a second-order Runge–Kutta method for temporal discretization. As the field continues to evolve, Peskin's research offers valuable insights and lays the groundwork for future advancements in applications of the Immersed Boundary method.

title: The coordination of arm movements: an experimentally confirmed mathematical model
abstract: This paper presents studies of the coordination of voluntary human arm movements. A mathematical model is formulated which is shown to predict both the qualitative features and the quantitative details observed experimentally in planar, multijoint arm movements. Coordination is modeled mathematically by defining an objective function, a measure of performance for any possible movement. The unique trajectory which yields the best performance is determined using dynamic optimization theory. In the work presented here, the objective function is the square of the magnitude of jerk (rate of change of acceleration) of the hand integrated over the entire movement. This is equivalent to assuming that a major goal of motor coordination is the production of the smoothest possible movement of the hand. Experimental observations of human subjects performing voluntary unconstrained movements in a horizontal plane are presented. They confirm the following predictions of the mathematical model: unconstrained point-to-point motions are approximately straight with bell-shaped tangential velocity profiles; curved motions (through an intermediate point or around an obstacle) have portions of low curvature joined by portions of high curvature; at points of high curvature, the tangential velocity is reduced; the durations of the low-curvature portions are approximately equal. The theoretical analysis is based solely on the kinematics of movement independent of the dynamics of the musculoskeletal system and is successful only when formulated in terms of the motion of the hand in extracorporal space. The implications with respect to movement organization are discussed.
summary:
Scientific Study Confirms Mathematical Model for Smooth Human Arm Movements

In a new study published in the Journal of Neuroscience, researchers Tamar Flash and Neville Hogan propose a mathematical model that predicts the qualitative and quantitative details observed in human arm movements. The model, focusing on the production of smooth hand movements, suggests that motor coordination aims to minimize jerk (rate of change of acceleration).

The results of the study show that unconstrained point-to-point motions are approximately straight with bell-shaped velocity profiles, while curved motions have low and high curvature segments. The theory is based on kinematics, independent of the dynamics of the musculoskeletal system, and is successful when considering the motion of the hand in extracorporal space.

The findings provide insights into movement organization and may contribute to a better understanding of motor control and coordination.

title: MuJoCo: A physics engine for model-based control
abstract: We describe a new physics engine tailored to model-based control. Multi-joint dynamics are represented in generalized coordinates and computed via recursive algorithms. Contact responses are computed via efficient new algorithms we have developed, based on the modern velocity-stepping approach which avoids the difficulties with spring-dampers. Models are specified using either a high-level C++ API or an intuitive XML file format. A built-in compiler transforms the user model into an optimized data structure used for runtime computation. The engine can compute both forward and inverse dynamics. The latter are well-defined even in the presence of contacts and equality constraints. The model can include tendon wrapping as well as actuator activation states (e.g. pneumatic cylinders or muscles). To facilitate optimal control applications and in particular sampling and finite differencing, the dynamics can be evaluated for different states and controls in parallel. Around 400,000 dynamics evaluations per second are possible on a 12-core machine, for a 3D homanoid with 18 dofs and 6 active contacts. We have already used the engine in a number of control applications. It will soon be made publicly available.
summary:
Title: New Physics Engine Accelerates Control of Robotic Systems

Authors Emanuel Todorov, Tom Erez, and Yuval Tassa have introduced a physics engine, dubbed MuJoCo, designed to streamline model-based control in robotics. The engine employs efficient algorithms to compute multi-joint dynamics and contact responses while avoiding the usual troubles with traditional spring-dampers.

Models of robotic systems can be specified through a user-friendly C++ API or XML file format, which are then compiled into an optimized structure for runtime calculation. The engine is capable of computing both forward and inverse dynamics, the latter being defined even when contacts and constraints occur. It also includes features for tendon wrapping and various actuator activation states to better represent complex robotic systems. Additionally, MuJoCo allows for parallel computation of dynamics across different states and controls, potentially evaluating around 400,000 dynamics calculations per second on a 12-core machine with a 3D humanoid robot having 18 degrees of freedom (DOF) and 6 active contacts. The researchers have already used the engine in multiple control applications and plan to make it publicly available soon.
topic: Dynamics and Control of Mechanical Systems
allAuthors: Emanuel Todorov; Tom Erez; Yuval Tassa

title: Angular Momentum in Quantum Mechanics
abstract: This book offers a concise introduction to the angular momentum, one of the most fundamental quantities in all of quantum mechanics. Beginning with the quantization of angular momentum, spin angular momentum, and the orbital angular momentum, the author goes on to discuss the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients for a two-component system. After developing the necessary mathematics, specifically spherical tensors and tensor operators, the author then investigates the 3-j, 6-j, and 9-j symbols. Throughout, the author provides practical applications to atomic, molecular, and nuclear physics. These include partial-wave expansions, the emission and absorption of particles, the proton and electron quadrupole moment, matrix element calculation in practice, and the properties of the symmetrical top molecule.
summary:
**Physics Today: Quantum Angular Momentum Exploration Extended**

In a new publication for Physics Today, authors A.R. Edmonds and H. Mendlowitz delve deeper into one of quantum mechanics' fundamental principles - angular momentum. This book offers a comprehensive yet concise introduction to the topic, starting with the quantization of both orbit and spin angular momentum.

The authors explore the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients for a two-component system, providing readers with theoretical foundations through spherical tensors and tensor operators. The discussion then expands to cover intricate 3-j, 6-j, and 9-j symbols - instrumental in atomic, molecular, and nuclear physics applications.

The work offers practical insights into partial-wave expansions, particle emission and absorption, properties of the symmetrical top molecule, matrix element calculations, proton and electron quadrupole moments, among other essential concepts. This valuable resource serves as a crucial stepping stone for researchers in fields such as quantum chemistry and nuclear physics.

title: Particle swarm optimization: developments, applications and resources
abstract: This paper focuses on the engineering and computer science aspects of developments, applications, and resources related to particle swarm optimization. Developments in the particle swarm algorithm since its origin in 1995 are reviewed. Included are brief discussions of constriction factors, inertia weights, and tracking dynamic systems. Applications, both those already developed, and promising future application areas, are reviewed. Finally, resources related to particle swarm optimization are listed, including books, Web sites, and software. A particle swarm optimization bibliography is at the end of the paper.
summary:
**Artificial Intelligence Paper Explores Advancements in Particle Swarm Algorithms**

In a recent publication, computer scientists Eberhart and Shi delve into the advancements, applications, and resources related to the popular problem-solving method known as particle swarm optimization (PSO). The paper reviews developments since PSO's introduction in 1995, discussing crucial factors like constriction factors, inertia weights, and tracking dynamic systems.

The authors also examine both existing applications and potential future ones, demonstrating the versatility of PSO in fields such as optimization problems in engineering and computer science. They offer an extensive list of resources for those interested in exploring PSO further, providing books, websites, and software to support ongoing research.

The paper closes with a comprehensive bibliography, offering a valuable starting point for anyone pursuing particle swarm optimization studies. By reviewing the rich history, current state, and promising future applications of this powerful algorithm, Eberhart and Shi encourage further exploration in the field of swarm behavior-based computational intelligence.

title: Weak elastic anisotropy
abstract: Abstract Most bulk elastic media are weakly anisotropic. The equations governing weak anisotropy are much simpler than those governing strong anisotropy, and they are much easier to grasp intuitively. These equations indicate that a certain anisotropic parameter (denoted delta ) controls most anisotropic phenomena of importance in exploration geophysics, some of which are nonnegligible even when the anisotropy is weak. The critical parameter delta is an awkward combination of elastic parameters, a combination which is totally independent of horizontal velocity and which may be either positive or negative in natural contexts.
summary:
Title: Simplified Physics of Weak Elastic Anisotropy

Journal: Geophysics

Author: Leon Thomsen

The study by Leon Thomsen focuses on the field of physics, particularly condensed matter physics and exploration geophysics. The researcher sheds light on weakly anisotropic elastic media, proposing that these have simpler governing equations compared to their strongly anisotropic counterparts. These equations reveal a critical parameter (delta), which plays a significant role in various anisotropic phenomena relevant to exploration geophysics, even when the anisotropy is weak. The study also emphasizes that the sign of this delta can be either positive or negative in natural contexts, offering new insights into the complexities of anisotropies in elastic media.

title: A generalized dynamical theory of thermoelasticity
abstract: AI abstract - This study presents a generalized dynamical theory of thermoelasticity, which combines mathematical analysis and classical mechanics to establish a comprehensive framework for understanding the behavior of materials under combined thermal and mechanical loads. Mathematics article published on Journal of Mechanics and Physics of Solids presents new dynamical theory of thermoelasticity

Lord and Yechiel Shulman have developed a generalized dynamical theory of thermoelasticity, blending mathematical analysis with classical mechanics to offer an extensive framework for understanding material behavior under complex thermal and mechanical stressors. title: Linear Models of Dissipation whose Q is almost Frequency Independent--II
abstract: Laboratory experiments and field observations indicate that the Q of many non-ferromagnetic inorganic solids is almost frequency independent in the range 10−2–107 c/s, although no single substance has been investigated over the entire frequency spectrum. One of the purposes of this investigation is to find the analytic expression for a linear dissipative mechanism whose Q is almost frequency independent over large frequency ranges. This will be obtained by introducing fractional derivatives in the stress-strain relation. Since the aim of this research is also to contribute to elucidating the dissipating mechanism in the Earth free modes, we shall treat the dissipation in the free, purely torsional, modes of a shell. The dissipation in a plane wave will also be treated. The theory is checked with the new values determined for the Q of spheroidal free modes of the Earth in the range between 10 and 5 min integrated with the Q of Rayleigh waves in the range between 5 and 0·6 min. Another check of the theory is made with the experimental values of the Q of the longitudinal waves in an aluminium rod in the range between 10−5 and 10−3 s. In both checks the theory represents the observed phenomena very satisfactorily. The time derivative which enters the stress-strain relation in both cases is of order 0·15. The present paper is a generalized version of another (Caputo 1966b) in which an elementary definition of some differential operators was used. In this paper we give also a rigorous proof of the formulae to be used in obtaining the analytic expression of Q; moreover, we present two checks of the theory with experimental data.
summary:
Headline:
New mathematical model offers insights into frequency-independent dissipation in solid materials

Summary:
Physics researcher Michèle Caputo has presented a new analytical expression for linear dissipative mechanisms that exhibit almost frequency-independent properties over large ranges, according to a paper published in the Geophysical Journal International. Caputo's work could provide insight into the dissipation mechanism in Earth's free modes and builds upon her previous research, which introduced fractional derivatives in stress-strain relations. The theory is validated by comparing with Q values of Earth's spheroidal free modes and aluminum rod longitudinal waves and performs satisfactorily, suggesting a time derivative of order 0.15 plays a significant role in the stress-strain relation.

title: A universal instability of many-dimensional oscillator systems
abstract: AI abstract - This study explores the universal instability inherent in many-dimensional oscillator systems, as presented by Chirikov in 1979 within the realm of classical mechanics and perturbed motion. The paper delves into the conditions under which these systems exhibit instability, providing insights relevant to a wide range of physical phenomena.
summary:
New Study Unveils Universal Instability in Complex Physics Systems

Physicist B. V. Chirikov's groundbreaking 1979 study published in Physics Reports sheds light on the universal instability found in many-dimensional oscillator systems, an area of classical mechanics and perturbed motion. The research offers insight into the conditions under which these complex systems become unstable, providing valuable perspectives for understanding various physical phenomena.

title: Space-Time Approach to Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics
abstract: Non-relativistic quantum mechanics is formulated here in a different way. It is, however, mathematically equivalent to the familiar formulation. In quantum mechanics the probability of an event which can happen in several different ways is the absolute square of a sum of complex contributions, one from each alternative way. The probability that a particle will be found to have a path $x(t)$ lying somewhere within a region of space time is the square of a sum of contributions, one from each path in the region. The contribution from a single path is postulated to be an exponential whose (imaginary) phase is the classical action (in units of $\ensuremath{\hbar}$) for the path in question. The total contribution from all paths reaching $x$, $t$ from the past is the wave function $\ensuremath{\psi}(x, t)$. This is shown to satisfy Schroedinger's equation. The relation to matrix and operator algebra is discussed. Applications are indicated, in particular to eliminate the coordinates of the field oscillators from the equations of quantum electrodynamics.
summary:
Title: Feynman Revolutionizes Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics

In a groundbreaking work published in Reviews of Modern Physics, physicist Richard P. Feynman proposes a fresh approach to non-relativistic quantum mechanics. This new formulation, mathematically equivalent to the traditional one, is based on the idea that the probability of an event occurring through various paths is the square of a complex sum of contributions, one from each alternative way.

Feynman's innovative concept posits that the contribution from a single path is an exponential whose phase is the classical action related to the path in question. This new formulation could simplify calculations in quantum electrodynamics and potentially lead to significant advancements in the field, as Feynman hints at in his paper.
primaryField: Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics

title: A Theory of the Linear Viscoelastic Properties of Dilute Solutions of Coiling Polymers
abstract: The necessary coordination of the motions of different parts of a polymer molecule is made the basis of a theory of the linear viscoelastic properties of dilute solutions of coiling polymers. This is accomplished by use of the concept of the submolecule, a portion of polymer chain long enough for the separation of its ends to approximate a Gaussian probability distribution. The configuration of a submolecule is specified in terms of the vector which corresponds to its end-to-end separation. The configuration of a molecule which contains N submolecules is described by the corresponding set of N vectors. The action of a velocity gradient disturbs the distribution of configurations of the polymer molecules away from its equilibrium form, storing free energy in the system. The coordinated thermal motions of the segments cause the configurations to drift toward their equilibrium distribution. The coordination is taken into account by the mathematical requirement that motions of the atom which joins two submolecules change the configurations of both submolecules. By means of an orthogonal transformation of coordinates, the coordination of all the motions of the parts of a molecule is resolved into a series of modes. Each mode has a characteristic relaxation time. The theory produces equations by means of which the relaxation times, the components of the complex viscosity, and the components of the complex rigidity can be calculated from the steady flow viscosities of the solution and the solvent, the molecular weight and concentration of the polymer, and the absolute temperature. Limitations of the theory may arise from the exclusion from consideration of (1) very rapid relaxation processes involving segments shorter than the submolecule and (2) the obstruction of the motion of a segment by other segments with which it happens to be in contact. Another possible cause of disagreement between the theory and experimental data is the polydispersity of any actual polymer; this factor is important because the calculated relaxation times increase rapidly with increasing molecular weight.
summary:
**Study proposes groundbreaking theory for understanding viscoelastic properties of dilute polymer solutions**

In a new paper published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, researcher Prince E. Rouse presents a novel theory that explains the linear viscoelastic properties of coiling polymers in dilute solutions. The theory is built upon the concept of a submolecule, a segment of polymer chain long enough for its ends to approximate a Gaussian probability distribution.

Using orthogonal transformation of coordinates, Rouse resolves all the motions of a polymer molecule into a series of modes, each with a unique relaxation time. The theory offers equations to calculate these relaxation times, complex viscosity components, and complex rigidity from relevant experimental data such as steady flow viscosities, molecular weight, concentration, and temperature.

The study aims to address the coordination among different parts of a polymer molecule, recognizing that rapid relaxation processes involving shorter segments and segment obstruction by other molecules require further exploration. Additionally, the potential cause for disagreement between the theory and experimental data may be due to polydispersity in actual polymers, as calculated relaxation times increase dramatically with molecular weight.

title: The Lattice Boltzmann Equation for Fluid Dynamics and Beyond
abstract: Abstract In recent years, certain forms of the Boltzmann equation--now going by the name of "Lattice Boltzmann equation" (LBE)--have emerged which relinquish most mathematical complexities of the true Boltzmann equation without sacrificing physical fidelity in the description of complex fluid motion. This book provides the first detailed survey of LBE theory and its major applications to date. Accessible to a broad audience of scientists dealing with complex system dynamics, the book also portrays future developments in allied areas of science where fluid motion plays a distinguished role.
summary:
**Headline:**
New Book Explores Lattice Boltzmann Equation, Revolutionizing Complex Fluid Dynamics

**Summary:**
In a groundbreaking work, renowned physicist Sauro Succi has authored a comprehensive book exploring the Lattice Boltzmann Equation (LBE), a modern form of the Boltzmann equation. This new approach simplifies complexities while maintaining accuracy in describing intricate fluid motion. The book serves as an accessible guide for scientists dealing with complex system dynamics, and hints at future advancements in related scientific fields where fluid motion plays a significant role.

title: Cosmological consequences of a rolling homogeneous scalar field
abstract: The cosmological consequences of a pervasive, rolling, self-interacting, homogeneous scalar field are investigated. A number of models in which the energy density of the scalar field red-shifts in a specific manner are studied. In these models the current epoch is chosen to be scalar-field dominated to agree with dynamical estimates of the density parameter, ${\ensuremath{\Omega}}_{\mathrm{dyn}\mathrm{\ensuremath{\sim}}0.2}$, and zero spatial curvature. The required scalar-field potential is ``nonlinear'' and decreases in magnitude as the value of the scalar field increases. A special solution of the field equations which is an attractive, time-dependent, fixed point is presented. These models are consistent with the classical tests of gravitation theory. The E\"otv\"os-Dicke measurements strongly constrain the coupling of the scalar field to light (nongravitational) fields. Nucleosynthesis proceeds as in the standard hot big-bang model. In linear perturbation theory the behavior of baryonic perturbations, in the baryon-dominated epoch, do not differ significantly from the canonical scenario, while the presence of a substantial amount of homogeneous scalar-field energy density at low red-shifts inhibits the growth of perturbations in the baryonic fluid. The energy density in the scalar field is not appreciably perturbed by nonrelativistic gravitational fields, either in the radiation-dominated, matter-dominated, or scalar-field-dominated epochs. On the basis of this effect, we argue that these models could reconcile the low dynamical estimates of the mean mass density with the negligibly small spatial curvature preferred by inflation.
summary:
Paper Proposes New Cosmological Models based on Rolling Scalar Field

Their research investigates models where the energy density of the scalar field declines in a specific way, aiming to align with contemporary estimates of the density parameter and zero spatial curvature.

These models, which are consistent with classical tests of general relativity, could potentially reconcile low dynamical mass density estimates with the negligible spatial curvature favored by inflationary theories. The Eotvos-Dicke measurements help constrain the coupling of the scalar field to non-gravitational fields, and nucleosynthesis proceeds as in the standard hot big-bang model.

The authors present a special solution of the field equations, which serves as an attractive, time-dependent, fixed point, and their work builds upon scalar theories of gravitation and inflationary cosmology, offering new directions for these areas of study.

title: Hydrodynamics of soft active matter
abstract: This review summarizes theoretical progress in the field of active matter, placing it in the context of recent experiments. This approach offers a unified framework for the mechanical and statistical properties of living matter: biofilaments and molecular motors in vitro or in vivo, collections of motile microorganisms, animal flocks, and chemical or mechanical imitations. A major goal of this review is to integrate several approaches proposed in the literature, from semimicroscopic to phenomenological. In particular, first considered are ``dry'' systems, defined as those where momentum is not conserved due to friction with a substrate or an embedding porous medium. The differences and similarities between two types of orientationally ordered states, the nematic and the polar, are clarified. Next, the active hydrodynamics of suspensions or ``wet'' systems is discussed and the relation with and difference from the dry case, as well as various large-scale instabilities of these nonequilibrium states of matter, are highlighted. Further highlighted are various large-scale instabilities of these nonequilibrium states of matter. Various semimicroscopic derivations of the continuum theory are discussed and connected, highlighting the unifying and generic nature of the continuum model. Throughout the review, the experimental relevance of these theories for describing bacterial swarms and suspensions, the cytoskeleton of living cells, and vibrated granular material is discussed. Promising extensions toward greater realism in specific contexts from cell biology to animal behavior are suggested, and remarks are given on some exotic active-matter analogs. Last, the outlook for a quantitative understanding of active matter, through the interplay of detailed theory with controlled experiments on simplified systems, with living or artificial constituents, is summarized.
summary:
**New Review Provides Comprehensive Look at "Active Matter" in Physics**

A new review published in Reviews of Modern Physics brings together essential theoretical progress in the field of active matter, a broad concept encompassing a wide range of systems from microorganisms and biofilaments to chemical or mechanical imitations.

Compiled by prominent physicists, including M. Cristina Marchetti, Jean-François Joanny, Sriraṁ Ramaswamy, Tanniemola B. Liverpool, Jacques Prost, Madan Rao, and Robert Simha, the review presents a unified framework for understanding the mechanical and statistical properties of living matter, from in vitro biological systems like molecular motors to animal flocks and chemical or mechanical mimics.

The study aims to integrate various approaches from semimicroscopic to phenomenological theories, with a focus on "dry" systems characterized by friction with a substrate or porous medium, and the differences and similarities between orientationally ordered states like nematic and polar. It also discusses active hydrodynamics in wet systems and highlights large-scale instabilities of these nonequilibrium states of matter.

The authors' connections among various semimicroscopic derivations of the continuum theory help emphasize its unifying nature, while the experimental relevance of these theories for complex systems like bacterial swarms and suspensions, the cytoskeleton of living cells, and vibrated granular materials is also explored.

Promising extensions are suggested toward greater realism in specific contexts, such as cell biology and animal behavior, and intriguing active-matter analogs are considered. Additionally, the outlook for a quantitative understanding of active matter through a blend of detailed theory with controlled experiments on simplified systems is summarized.

title: The density functional formalism, its applications and prospects
abstract: A scheme that reduces the calculations of ground-state properties of systems of interacting particles exactly to the solution of single-particle Hartree-type equations has obvious advantages. It is not surprising, then, that the density functional formalism, which provides a way of doing this, has received much attention in the past two decades. The quality of the energy surfaces calculated using a simple local-density approximation for exchange and correlation exceeds by far the original expectations. In this work, the authors survey the formalism and some of its applications (in particular to atoms and small molecules) and discuss the reasons for the successes and failures of the local-density approximation and some of its modifications.
summary:
Title: Groundbreaking Physics Theory Streamlines Complex Particle Calculations

A new theoretical framework, the density functional formalism, has been gaining significant attention in physics over the past two decades for its ability to simplify calculations of ground-state properties of interacting particles. The scheme reduces these complex calculations to solving single-particle Hartree-type equations, making it an attractive choice for scientists worldwide.

The authors of this study, R. Jones and O. Gunnarsson, elaborate on the formalism's applications, focusing on atomic and small molecule systems. They credit its success to the quality of energy surfaces calculated using a simple local-density approximation for exchange and correlation, exceeding initial expectations.

In their review, the authors also discuss the reasons behind the approach's achievements as well as its limitations, offering insights that could lead to refinements in this promising methodology.

title: Empirical study of particle swarm optimization
abstract: We empirically study the performance of the particle swarm optimizer (PSO). Four different benchmark functions with asymmetric initial range settings are selected as testing functions. The experimental results illustrate the advantages and disadvantages of the PSO. Under all the testing cases, the PSO always converges very quickly towards the optimal positions but may slow its convergence speed when it is near a minimum. Nevertheless, the experimental results show that the PSO is a promising optimization method and a new approach is suggested to improve PSO's performance near the optima, such as using an adaptive inertia weight.

title: Molecular dynamics with electronic transitions
abstract: A method is proposed for carrying out molecular dynamics simulations of processes that involve electronic transitions. The time dependent electronic Schrödinger equation is solved self-consistently with the classical mechanical equations of motion of the atoms. At each integration time step a decision is made whether to switch electronic states, according to probabilistic ‘‘fewest switches’’ algorithm. If a switch occurs, the component of velocity in the direction of the nonadiabatic coupling vector is adjusted to conserve energy. The procedure allows electronic transitions to occur anywhere among any number of coupled states, governed by the quantum mechanical probabilities. The method is tested against accurate quantal calculations for three one-dimensional, two-state models, two of which have been specifically designed to challenge any such mixed classical–quantal dynamical theory. Although there are some discrepancies, initial indications are encouraging. The model should be applicable to a wide variety of gas-phase and condensed-phase phenomena occurring even down to thermal energies.

Encouraging results are shown from initial tests, despite some discrepancies with quantal calculations. title: Progress in the development of a Reynolds-stress turbulence closure
abstract: The paper develops proposals for a model of turbulence in which the Reynolds stresses are determined from the solution of transport equations for these variables and for the turbulence energy dissipation rate ε. Particular attention is given to the approximation of the pressure-strain correlations; the forms adopted appear to give reasonably satisfactory partitioning of the stresses both near walls and in free shear flows. Numerical solutions of the model equations are presented for a selection of strained homogeneous shear flows and for two-dimensional inhomogeneous shear flows including the jet, the wake, the mixing layer and plane channel flow. In addition, it is shown that the closure does predict a very strong influence of secondary strain terms for flow over curved surfaces.

title: The motion of ellipsoidal particles immersed in a viscous fluid
abstract: Abstract In both physical and biological science, we are often concerned with the properties of a fluid, or plasma, in which small particles or corpuscles are suspended and carried about by the motion of the fluid. The presence of the particles will influence the properties of the suspension in bulk, and, in particular, its viscosity will be increased. The most complete mathematical treatment of the problem, from this point of view, has been that given by Einstein, who considered the case of spherical particles and gave a simple formula for the increase in the viscosity. We have extended this work to the case of particles of ellipsoidal shape. The second section of the paper is occupied with the requisite solution of the equations of motion of the fluid. The problem of the motion of a viscous fluid, due to an ellipsoid moving through it with a small velocity of translation in a direction parallel to one of its axes, has been solved by Oberbeck, and the corresponding problem for an ellipsoid rotating about one of its axes by Edwards. In both cases the equations of motion are approximated by neglecting the terms involving the squares of the velocities. It may be seen, a posteriori, that the condition for the validity of this approximation is that the product of the velocity of the ellipsoid by its linear dimensions shall be small compared with the “kinematic coefficient, of viscosity” of the fluid. In relation to our present problem, it will therefore be satisfied either for sufficiently slow motions, or for sufficiently small particles.
summary:
Mathematical study on fluid motion featuring ellipsoidal particles

Building on Einstein's work about spherical particles, this study expands to ellipsoid-shaped subjects, focusing on their effect on a viscous liquid’s bulk viscosity. The paper presents a solution for the motion equations of fluids near ellipsoidal bodies at slow speeds or with small particle dimensions. This research aims to broaden our understanding of the complex dynamics between viscous liquids and three-dimensional particles, advancing classical mechanics in fluid dynamics.

title: Mechanics of Deformation and Acoustic Propagation in Porous Media
abstract: A unified treatment of the mechanics of deformation and acoustic propagation in porous media is presented, and some new results and generalizations are derived. The writer's earlier theory of deformation of porous media derived from general principles of nonequilibrium thermodynamics is applied. The fluid-solid medium is treated as a complex physical-chemical system with resultant relaxation and viscoelastic properties of a very general nature. Specific relaxation models are discussed, and the general applicability of a correspondence principle is further emphasized. The theory of acoustic propagation is extended to include anisotropic media, solid dissipation, and other relaxation effects. Some typical examples of sources of dissipation other than fluid viscosity are considered.
summary: In the realm of Porous Media research, a groundbreaking study by M. A. The focus is on treating fluid-solid media as complex systems exhibiting relaxation and viscoelastic properties. Various relaxation models are discussed, reinforcing the correspondence principle's applicability. Additionally, the study extends acoustic propagation theory to accommodate anisotropic media, solid dissipation, and other relaxation effects, shedding light on alternative sources of dissipation beyond fluid viscosity.

title: Angular Momentum in Quantum Mechanics
abstract: This book offers a concise introduction to the angular momentum, one of the most fundamental quantities in all of quantum mechanics. title: Hydromagnetic flows from accretion discs and the production of radio jets
abstract: We examine the possibility that energy and angular momentum are removed magnetically from accretion discs, by field lines that leave the disc surface and extend to large distances. We illustrate this mechanism by solving the equations of magnetohydrodynamics, assuming infinite conductivity, for axially symmetric, self-similar, cold magnetospheric flow from a Keplerian accretion disc in which the field strength B scales with radius r as |$B\,\propto\,{r}^{-5/4}$.| We show that a centrifugally driven outflow of matter from the disc is possible, if the poloidal component of the magnetic field makes an angle of less than 60° with the disc surface. At large distances from the disc, the toroidal component of the magnetic field becomes important and collimates the outflow into a pair of anti-parallel jets moving perpendicular to the disc. Close to the disc, the flow is probably driven by gas pressure in a hot magnetically dominated corona. In this way, magnetic stresses can extract the angular momentum from a thin accretion disc and thus enable matter to be accreted, independently of the presence of viscosity. These jet solutions have the property that most of the power is concentrated within a central core, while most of the angular momentum and magnetic flux is carried near the jet walls. The relevance of this mechanism for the evolution of accretion discs around massive black holes in galactic nuclei and the production of jets in extragalactic radio sources is described.
summary:
"New Space Study Suggests Accretion Discs Drive Radio Jets"

In a new study published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, physicists R. D. Blandford and D. G. Payne propose a mechanism to explain how energy and angular momentum can be extracted from accretion discs surrounding black holes, leading to the production of radio jets.

The researchers solve complex equations of magnetohydrodynamics for an axially symmetric, cold flow, assuming infinite conductivity and a specific scaling relation for the magnetic field strength with radius in a Keplerian accretion disc. The team finds that if the poloidal component of the magnetic field makes an angle of less than 60 degrees with the disc surface, it is possible to drive an outflow of matter from the disc. This outflow becomes collimated into a pair of anti-parallel jets moving perpendicular to the disc at large distances, potentially powering extragalactic radio sources and aiding the gravitational accretion process without the need for viscosity.
journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

title: cosmological simulation code GADGET
abstract: We present a novel numerical implementation of radiative transfer in the cosmological smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation code GADGET. It is based on a fast, robust and photon-conserving integration scheme where the radiation transport problem is approximated in terms of moments of the transfer equation and by using a variable Eddington tensor as a closure relation, following the ‘OTVET’-suggestion of Gnedin &amp; Abel. We derive a suitable anisotropic diffusion operator for use in the SPH discretization of the local photon transport, and we combine this with an implicit solver that guarantees robustness and photon conservation. This entails a matrix inversion problem of a huge, sparsely populated matrix that is distributed in memory in our parallel code. We solve this task iteratively with a conjugate gradient scheme. Finally, to model photon sink processes we consider ionisation and recombination processes of hydrogen, which is represented with a chemical network that is evolved with an implicit time integration scheme. We present several tests of our implementation, including single and multiple sources in static uniform density fields with and without temperature evolution, shadowing by a dense clump, and multiple sources in a static cosmological density field. All tests agree quite well with analytical computations or with predictions from other radiative transfer codes, except for shadowing. However, unlike most other radiative transfer codes presently in use for studying reionisation, our new method can be used on-the-fly during dynamical cosmological simulation, allowing simultaneous treatments of galaxy formation and the reionisation process of the Universe. Key words: radiative transfer- methods: numerical
summary:
Title: New Cosmological Simulation Code GADGET Offers Real-Time Reionization Study

In a groundbreaking development in the field of physics, Volker Springel presents a novel implementation in the cosmological smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation code GADGET. The new feature is a numerical solution for radiative transfer, which addresses the transport of light in the universe during reionization.

The radiation problem is tackled using moments of the transfer equation and a closure relation based on the 'OTVET' suggestion by Gnedin & Abel. A suitable anisotropic diffusion operator has been developed for use in the SPH discretization of local photon transport, backed by an implicit solver ensuring robustness and photon conservation.

This revolutionary development addresses a significant challenge – solving matrix inversion problems of large, sparsely populated matrices in parallel code through iterative conjugate gradient schemes. The new method stands out due to its ability to simultaneously explore galaxy formation and the reionization process during dynamic cosmological simulations, offering unprecedented insights into the cosmic era of reionization.

title: A Joint Coordinate System for the Clinical Description of Three-Dimensional Motions: Application to the Knee
abstract: The experimental study of joint kinematics in three dimensions requires the description and measurement of six motion components. An important aspect of any method of description is the ease with which it is communicated to those who use the data. This paper presents a joint coordinate system that provides a simple geometric description of the three-dimensional rotational and translational motion between two rigid bodies. The coordinate system is applied to the knee and related to the commonly used clinical terms for knee joint motion. A convenient characteristic of the coordinate system shared by spatial linkages is that large joint displacements are independent of the order in which the component translations and rotations occur.
summary:
New Joint Coordinate System Simplifies Three-Dimensional Motion Analysis: Researchers Propose Solutions for Complex Knee Movements

In the Journal of Biomechanical Engineering, Edward S. Grood and Wilfredo J. Suntay present a new joint coordinate system to streamline the description and measurement of complex three-dimensional motions, focusing on joint kinematics, particularly in the knee. This advanced method provides simple geometric insights into rotational and translational movements between two rigid bodies, addressing issues with current data communication challenges in clinical terms.

By applying this new coordinate system to knee joint motion, large displacements can be easily understood without being dependent on the order of component translations or rotations, offering a significant advantage for future research studies on gait analysis and rehabilitation technologies within computer science.

title: The world as a hologram
abstract: According to ’t Hooft the combination of quantum mechanics and gravity requires the three-dimensional world to be an image of data that can be stored on a two-dimensional projection much like a holographic image. The two-dimensional description only requires one discrete degree of freedom per Planck area and yet it is rich enough to describe all three-dimensional phenomena. After outlining ’t Hooft’s proposal we give a preliminary informal description of how it may be implemented. One finds a basic requirement that particles must grow in size as their momenta are increased far above the Planck scale. The consequences for high-energy particle collisions are described. The phenomenon of particle growth with momentum was previously discussed in the context of string theory and was related to information spreading near black hole horizons. The considerations of this paper indicate that the effect is much more rapid at all but the earliest times. In fact the rate of spreading is found to saturate the bound from causality. Finally we consider string theory as a possible realization of ’t Hooft’s idea. The light front lattice string model of Klebanov and Susskind is reviewed and its similarities with the holographic theory are demonstrated. The agreement between the two requires unproven but plausible assumptions about the nonperturbative behavior of string theory. Very similar ideas to those in this paper have long been held by Charles Thorn.
summary:
Paper proposes a groundbreaking notion: Our three-dimensional world could be a hologram, as outlined by 't Hooft's hypothesis. By storing data on a two-dimensional projection, the theory reduces the complexity of describing physical phenomena.

The study sheds light on particle growth with increased momentum, a phenomenon previously linked to string theory and black hole horizons. Remarkably, findings suggest this rapid expansion occurs not just near black holes, but across all time frames, saturating causality's bounds.

The paper also examines string theory as a potential realization of 't Hooft's idea, drawing parallels between the holographic theory and the light front lattice string model by Klebanov and Susskind. However, the agreement requires assumptions about string theory's nonperturbative behavior that remain unproven yet plausible. These ideas echo long-held theories proposed by Charles Thorn.

title: Kinetics of thermal degradation of char‐forming plastics from thermogravimetry. Application to a phenolic plastic
abstract: Abstract A technique was devised for obtaining rate laws and kinetic parameters which describe the thermal degradation of plastics from TGA data. The method is based on the inter‐comparison of experiments which were performed at different linear rates of heating. By this method it is possible to determine the activation energy of certain professes without knowing the form of the kinetic equation. This technique was applied to fiberglass‐reinforced CTL 91‐LD phenolic resin, where the rate law ‐ (1/ w e )( dw/dt ) = 10 18 e −55,000/ RT [( w ‐ w f )/ w 0 ,] 5 , nr. −1 , was found to apply to a major part of the degradation. The equation was successfully tested by several techniques, including a comparison with constant temperature data that were available in the literature. The activation energy was thought to be correct within 10 kcal.
summary:
Title: Novel Thermogravimetry Method Accurately Determines Degradation of Phenolic Plastic

In a groundbreaking study published by Henry L. Friedman in Journal of Polymer Science Part C Polymer Symposia, a new method for measuring the thermal degradation rate of plastics using Thermogravimetry (TGA) has been developed. The innovative approach allows for determining the activation energy without requiring knowledge of complex kinetic equations.

Friedman's technique was applied to a specific phenolic plastic, CTL 91-LD, and a significant discovery was made regarding its degradation rate law, which can be represented as (1/w e) (dw/dt) = 10^18 e^-55,000/RT [(w - w f)/w0]^5, nr.-1. While more research is needed for confirmation and broader application, this study lays important groundwork for understanding the degradation of char-forming plastics like phenolic resin, offering potential solutions to telecommunications-related degradation issues.
journal: Journal of Polymer Science Part C Polymer Symposia

title: Simulating Microscopic Hydrodynamic Phenomena with Dissipative Particle Dynamics
abstract: We present a novel method for simulating hydrodynamic phenomena. This particle-based method combines features from molecular dynamics and lattice-gas automata. It is shown theoretically as well as in simulations that a quantitative description of isothermal Navier-Stokes flow is obtained with relatively few particles. Computationally, the method is much faster than molecular dynamics, and the at same time it is much more flexible than lattice-gas automata schemes.
summary:
Title: Groundbreaking Simulation Method Streamlines Study of Microscopic Hydrodynamic Phenomena

Sub-headline: Dissipative Particle Dynamics bridges gap between molecular dynamics and lattice gas automata for faster, more flexible simulations

Report: In a recent publication in Europhysics Letters (EPL), scientists Hoogerbrugge and Koelman introduced a novel approach to simulating microscopic hydrodynamic phenomena. This method, known as Dissipative Particle Dynamics (DPD), effectively merges elements of molecular dynamics and lattice-gas automata, allowing for a more efficient and adaptable simulation process compared to traditional methods.

The innovative technique offers the advantage of quantitatively describing isothermal Navier-Stokes flow with only a modest number of particles, making it a valuable tool in the study of these complex, fluid dynamic processes. The work by Hoogerbrugge and Koelman not only adds to the broader field of computational physics but also opens new paths for research by providing improved tools for simulations in this area.

title: Forces in Molecules
abstract: Formulas have been developed to calculate the forces in a molecular system directly, rather than indirectly through the agency of energy. This permits an independent calculation of the slope of the curves of energy vs. position of the nuclei, and may thus increase the accuracy, or decrease the labor involved in the calculation of these curves. The force on a nucleus in an atomic system is shown to be just the classical electrostatic force that would be exerted on this nucleus by other nuclei and by the electrons' charge distribution. Qualitative implications of this are discussed.

The force acting on a nucleus is revealed to be equivalent to the classical electrostatic force exerted by other nuclei and the distribution of electrons' charges (Atomic Physics). title: Engineering seismic risk analysis
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a method for the evaluation of the seismic risk at the site of an engineering project. The results are in terms of a ground motion parameter (such as peak acceleration) versus average return period. The method incorporates the influence of all potential sources of earthquakes and the average activity rates assigned to them. Arbitrary geographical relationships between the site and potential point, line, or areal sources can be modeled with computational ease. In the range of interest, the derived distributions of maximum annual ground motions are in the form of Type I or Type II extreme value distributions, if the more commonly assumed magnitude distribution and attenuation laws are used.
summary:
Title: New method for evaluating seismic risk at engineering sites

In the latest study published by Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, engineer C. Allin Cornell presents a novel approach to assessing seismic risk at construction sites. The new method considers all potential earthquake sources and their average rates of activity, accounting for arbitrary geographical relationships between the site and these sources.

By employing Type I or Type II extreme value distributions, the approach offers predictions in terms of ground motion parameters such as peak acceleration versus average return period. This groundbreaking research has the potential to significantly improve seismic risk analysis during engineering project planning and design stages.

title: Some Comments on the Evaluation of Model Performance
abstract: Quantitative approaches to the evaluation of model performance were recently examined by Fox (1981). His recommendations are briefly reviewed and a revised set of performance statistics is proposed. It is suggested that the correlation between model-predicted and observed data, commonly described by Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient, is an insufficient and often misleading measure of accuracy. A complement of difference and summary univariate indices is presented as the nucleus of a more informative, albeit fundamentally descriptive, approach to model evaluation. Two models that estimate monthly evapotranspiration are comparatively evaluated in order to illustrate how the recommended method(s) can be applied.

title: Black hole in three-dimensional spacetime
abstract: The standard Einstein-Maxwell equations in 2+1 spacetime dimensions, with a negative cosmological constant, admit a black hole solution. The 2+1 black hole---characterized by mass, angular momentum, and charge, defined by flux integrals at infinity---is quite similar to its 3+1 counterpart. Anti--de Sitter space appears as a negative energy state separated by a mass gap from the continuous black hole spectrum. Evaluation of the partition function yields that the entropy is equal to twice the perimeter length of the horizon.
summary:
Title: Physicists find three-dimensional black hole analog in lower dimensions

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review Letters, an international team of researchers have discovered a remarkable similarity between a three-dimensional black hole and its counterpart in lower dimensions. Led by Máximo Bañados, Claudio Teitelboim, and Jorge Zanelli, the investigation into 2+1 spacetime has revealed that Einstein-Maxwell equations with negative cosmological constant yield a black hole solution akin to its 3+1 counterpart. This two-dimensional black hole exhibits mass, angular momentum, and charge and is similar in many aspects.
The team discovered that the anti--de Sitter space appears as a negative energy state separating a mass gap from the continuous black hole spectrum, echoing the general relativistic properties of higher dimensional black holes. Furthermore, their calculations indicate an intriguing link between the black hole's entropy and the horizon's perimeter length in this two-dimensional spacetime scenario. This research not only advances our understanding of black holes in lower dimensions but also offers new insight into fundamental areas of theoretical physics such as quantum gravity and holography.

title: A Measure of Asymptotic Efficiency for Tests of a Hypothesis Based on the sum of Observations
abstract: In many cases an optimum or computationally convenient test of a simple hypothesis $H_0$ against a simple alternative $H_1$ may be given in the following form. Reject $H_0$ if $S_n = \sum^n_{j=1} X_j \leqq k,$ where $X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_n$ are $n$ independent observations of a chance variable $X$ whose distribution depends on the true hypothesis and where $k$ is some appropriate number. In particular the likelihood ratio test for fixed sample size can be reduced to this form. It is shown that with each test of the above form there is associated an index $\rho$. If $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ are the indices corresponding to two alternative tests $e = \log \rho_1/\log \rho_2$ measures the relative efficiency of these tests in the following sense. For large samples, a sample of size $n$ with the first test will give about the same probabilities of error as a sample of size $en$ with the second test. To obtain the above result, use is made of the fact that $P(S_n \leqq na)$ behaves roughly like $m^n$ where $m$ is the minimum value assumed by the moment generating function of $X - a$. It is shown that if $H_0$ and $H_1$ specify probability distributions of $X$ which are very close to each other, one may approximate $\rho$ by assuming that $X$ is normally distributed.
summary:
Mathematics Paper Proposes Efficiency Index for Statistical Tests

In a new paper published in The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, Herman Chernoff introduces an efficiency index for statistical tests that could streamline the process of comparing alternative methods in determining sample sizes.

Chernoff's work builds on the likelihood ratio test for fixed sample sizes and demonstrates how various tests of a simple hypothesis can be reduced to a unified form, relying on the sum of independent observations from a chance variable X. This index, or $\rho$, offers a means to gauge the relative efficiency of different tests, with larger values indicating more effective tests over large samples.

The mathematical foundation for this breakthrough lies in recognizing that the probability distribution of a sum of independent observations tends toward a power law in large sample sizes, with the key being the minimum value assumed by the moment generating function of X minus a constant (a). The paper further suggests an approximation for $\rho$ when the probability distributions of X under the null and alternative hypotheses are very similar—assuming normality of X can provide useful insights.

title: Reversible multiple time scale molecular dynamics
abstract: The Trotter factorization of the Liouville propagator is used to generate new reversible molecular dynamics integrators. This strategy is applied to derive reversible reference system propagator algorithms (RESPA) that greatly accelerate simulations of systems with a separation of time scales or with long range forces. The new algorithms have all of the advantages of previous RESPA integrators but are reversible, and more stable than those methods. These methods are applied to a set of paradigmatic systems and are shown to be superior to earlier methods. It is shown how the new RESPA methods are related to predictor–corrector integrators. Finally, we show how these methods can be used to accelerate the integration of the equations of motion of systems with Nosé thermostats.
summary:
Scientific Breakthrough: New Molecular Dynamics Integrators Offer Accelerated Simulations

In a groundbreaking study published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, researchers Mark E. Tuckerman, B. J. Berne, and Glenn Martyna reveal the development of new molecular dynamics integrators that can significantly speed up simulations for systems with varying time scales or long-range forces.

These innovative algorithms, known as reversible reference system propagator algorithms (RESPA), build upon the Trotter factorization of the Liouville propagator and improve upon existing RESPA methods by offering increased stability and reversibility.
