title: The law of the wake in the turbulent boundary layer
abstract: After an extensive survey of mean-velocity profile measurements in various two-dimensional incompressible turbulent boundary-layer flows, it is proposed to represent the profile by a linear combination of two universal functions. One is the well-known law of the wall. The other, called the law of the wake, is characterized by the profile at a point of separation or reattachment. These functions are considered to be established empirically, by a study of the mean-velocity profile, without reference to any hypothetical mechanism of turbulence. Using the resulting complete analytic representation for the mean-velocity field, the shearing-stress field for several flows is computed from the boundary-layer equations and compared with experimental data. The development of a turbulent boundary layer is ultimately interpreted in terms of an equivalent wake profile, which supposedly represents the large-eddy structure and is a consequence of the constraint provided by inertia. This equivalent wake profile is modified by the presence of a wall, at which a further constraint is provided by viscosity. The wall constraint, although it penetrates the entire boundary layer, is manifested chiefly in the sublayer flow and in the logarithmic profile near the wall. Finally, it is suggested that yawed or three-dimensional flows may be usefully represented by the same two universal functions, considered as vector rather than scalar quantities. If the wall component is defined to be in the direction of the surface shearing stress, then the wake component, at least in the few cases studied, is found to be very nearly parallel to the gradient of the pressure.
summary:
Scientific Paper: "A New 'Law of the Wake' Unveiled in Turbulent Boundary Layers"

In a groundbreaking study published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics, renowned physicist Donald Coles has proposed a novel approach to understanding turbulence in two-dimensional boundary layers. The paper, titled "The law of the wake in the turbulent boundary layer", introduces the 'law of the wake', complementing the existing 'law of the wall'.

Coles' study, drawing on extensive data from various turbulent flows, suggests representing the mean-velocity profile using a combination of these two universal functions. The 'law of the wake' is characterized by the profile at points of separation or reattachment, offering a new perspective and analytical representation for the mean-velocity field in boundary layers.

The findings could potentially revolutionize our understanding of turbulence and its impact on various fields, including aerodynamics and fluid mechanics, by providing a framework to interpret complex flow patterns in terms of an 'equivalent wake profile'. This profile represents the large-eddy structure and offers insight into the role of inertia and viscosity in boundary layer development.

Coles also hints at possible applications of this model for yawed or three-dimensional flows, suggesting that these functions could be extended to vector quantities, offering promising avenues for future research.

title: Large Amplitude Elastic Motions in Proteins from a Single-Parameter, Atomic Analysis
abstract: Normal mode analysis (NMA) is a leading method for studying long-time dynamics and elasticity of biomolecules. The method proceeds from complex semiempirical potentials characterizing the covalent and noncovalent interactions between atoms. It is widely accepted that such detailed potentials are essential to the success of NMA's. We show that a single-parameter potential is sufficient to reproduce the slow dynamics in good detail. Costly and inaccurate energy minimizations are eliminated, permitting direct analysis of crystal coordinates. The technique can be used for new applications, such as mapping of one crystal form to another by means of slow modes, and studying anomalous dynamics of large proteins and complexes.
summary:
Title: Revolutionary Single-Parameter Analysis Simplifies Elasticity Study in Proteins
Subheading: Physicist's Innovative Approach Cutts Down Complexity in Biomolecule Research

title: On the Relative Importance of the Driving Forces of Plate Motion
abstract: A number of possible mechanisms have recently been proposed for driving the motions of the lithospheric plates, such as pushing from mid-ocean ridges, pulling by downgoing slabs, suction toward trenches, and coupling of the plates to flow in the mantle. We advance a new observational method of testing these theories of the driving mechanism. Our basic approach is to solve the inverse problem of determining the relative strength of the plausible driving forces, given the observed motions and geometries of the lithospheric plates. Since the inertia of the plates is negligible, each plate must be in dynamic equilibrium, so that the sum of the torques acting on a plate must be zero. Thus, our problem is to determine the relative sizes of the forces that minimize the components of net torque on each plate. The results indicate that the forces acting on the downgoing slab control the velocity of the oceanic plates and are an order of magnitude stronger than any other force. Namely, all the oceanic plates attached to substantial amounts of downgoing slabs move with a ' terminal velocity ' at which the gravitational body force pulling the slabs downward is nearly balanced with the resistance acting on the slab; regardless of the other features of the trailing horizontal part of the plates. The drag on the bottom of the plates which resist motion is stronger under the continents than under the oceans.
summary:

The researchers propose a novel method to evaluate these theories by solving an inverse problem, determining the relative strength of potential mechanical drivers that cause plate movement.

Their analysis suggests that downgoing slabs play a significant role in controlling oceanic plate velocities. These forces are reported to be an order of magnitude stronger than other factors influencing plate motion, indicating the importance of the 'terminal velocity' at which gravitational body force and resistance act upon submerged slabs. The study also finds that drag on the underside of the plates is stronger beneath continents compared to oceans.

This research significantly advances our understanding of plate motion dynamics within geology, providing a key perspective on the driving forces behind this complex phenomenon.

abstract: We present a novel experimental method to measure linear viscoelastic moduli of complex fluids using dynamic light scattering. This method probes the moduli over a greatly extended frequency range and provides significant new insight into the elastic susceptibility of complex fluids.

title: Configurations of fluid membranes and vesicles
abstract: Abstract Vesicles consisting of a bilayer membrane of amphiphilic lipid molecules are remarkably flexible surfaces that show an amazing variety of shapes of different symmetry and topology. Owing to the fluidity of the membrane, shape transitions such as budding can be induced by temperature changes or the action of optical tweezers. Thermally excited shape fluctuations are both strong and slow enough to be visible by video microscopy. Depending on the physical conditions, vesicles adhere to and unbind from each other or a substrate. This article describes the systematic physical theory developed to understand the static and dynamic aspects of membrane and vesicle configurations. The preferred shapes arise from a competition between curvature energy, which derives from the bending elasticity of the membrane, geometrical constraints such as fixed surface area and fixed enclosed volume, and a signature of the bilayer aspect. These shapes of lowest energy are arranged into phase diagrams, which separate regions of different symmetry by continuous or discontinuous transitions. The geometrical constraints affect the fluctuations around these shapes by creating an effective tension. For vesicles of non-spherical topology, the conformal invariance of the curvature energy leads to conformal diffusion, which signifies a one-fold degeneracy of the ground state. Unbinding and adhesion transitions arise from the balance between attractive interactions and entropic repulsion or a cost in bending energy, respectively. Both the dynamics of equilibrium fluctuations and the dynamics of shape transformations are governed not only by viscous damping in the surrounding liquid but also by internal friction if the two monolayers slip over each other. More complex membranes such as that of the red blood cell exhibit a variety of new phenomena because of coupling between internal degrees of freedom and external geometry.
summary:
In the journal Advances In Physics, researcher Udo Seifert explores the intricate world of fluid vesicles, particularly focusing on their remarkable adaptability, curvature, and behavior under various conditions. The study builds upon previous work regarding vesicle shape transitions induced by temperature, optical tweezers, and membrane curvature.

The paper offers a comprehensive physical theory to understand the static and dynamic aspects of fluid membranes and vesicles, providing insights into the formation of preferred shapes influenced by factors such as membrane elasticity, geometrical constraints, and bilayer properties. These shape configurations are arranged in phase diagrams, which delineate regions of different symmetry through continuous or discontinuous transitions.

Seifert's findings reveal that complex interactions between the internal structure of vesicles and their external geometry result in various new phenomena, such as conformal diffusion in non-spherical vesicles. The research also illuminates factors governing both the dynamics of equilibrium fluctuations and shape transformations, with implications for more intricate membranes like that of red blood cells.

title: On kinematic waves I. Flood movement in long rivers
abstract: Abstract In this paper and in part II, we give the theory of a distinctive type of wave motion, which arises in any one-dimensional flow problem when there is an approximate functional relation at each point between the flow q (quantity passing a given point in unit time) and concentration k (quantity per unit distance). The wave property then follows directly from the equation of continuity satisfied by q and k. In view of this, these waves are described as ‘kinematic’, as distinct from the classical wave motions, which depend also on Newton’s second law of motion and are therefore called ‘dynamic’. Kinematic waves travel with the velocity dq/dk, and the flow q remains constant on each kinematic wave. Since the velocity of propagation of each wave depends upon the value of q carried by it, successive waves may coalesce to form ‘kinematic shock waves ’. From the point of view of kinematic wave theory, there is a discontinuous increase in q at a shock, but in reality a shock wave is a relatively narrow region in which (owing to the rapid increase of q) terms neglected by the flow concentration relation become important. The general properties of kinematic waves and shock waves are discussed in detail in §1. One example included in §1 is the interpretation of the group-velocity phenomenon in a dispersive medium as a particular case of the kinematic wave phenomenon. The remainder of part I is devoted to a detailed treatment of flood movement in long rivers, a problem in which kinematic waves play the leading role although dynamic waves (in this case, the long gravity waves) also appear. First (§2), we consider the variety of factors which can influence the approximate flow-concentration relation, and survey the various formulae which have been used in attempts to describe it. Then follows a more mathematical section (§3) in which the role of the dynamic waves is clarified. From the full equations of motion for an idealized problem it is shown that at the ‘Froude numbers’ appropriate to flood waves, the dynamic waves are rapidly attenuated and the main disturbance is carried downstream by the kinematic waves; some account is then given of the behaviour of the flow at higher Froude numbers. Also in §3, the full equations of motion are used to investigate the structure of the kinematic shock; for this problem, the shock is the ‘monoclinal flood wave’ which is well known in the literature of this subject. The final sections (§§4 and 5) contain the application of the theory of kinematic waves to the determination of flood movement. In §4 it is shown how the waves (including shock waves) travelling downstream from an observation point may be deduced from a knowledge of the variation with time of the flow at the observation point; this section then concludes with a brief account of the effect on the waves of tributaries and run-off. In §5, the modifications (similar to diffusion effects) which arise due to the slight dependence of the flow-concentration curve on the rate of change of flow or concentration, are described and methods for their inclusion in the theory are given.

title: Observing the State of a Linear System
abstract: In much of modern control theory designs are based on the assumption that the state vector of the system to be controlled is available for measurement. In many practical situations only a few output quantities are available. Application of theories which assume that the state vector is known is severely limited in these cases. In this paper it is shown that the state vector of a linear system can be reconstructed from observations of the system inputs and outputs. It is shown that the observer, which reconstructs the state vector, is itself a linear system whose complexity decreases as the number of output quantities available increases. The observer may be incorporated in the control of a system which does not have its state vector available for measurement. The observer supplies the state vector, but at the expense of adding poles to the over-all system.
summary:
Title: Observer Developed for Linear Systems Aids Control Without Full State Vector

In the journal IEEE Transactions on Military Electronics, researcher David G. Luenberger presents a groundbreaking concept that expands the scope of modern control theory. The paper, titled "Observing the State of a Linear System," focuses on situations where only limited output quantities are available, thus hindering the application of theories assuming full state vector knowledge.

Luenberger introduces an observer, a linear system, designed to reconstruct the full state vector from observations of both inputs and outputs of a linear system. The complexity of this observer decreases as the number of available output quantities increases, opening new possibilities for systems without a readily available state vector. While the use of the observer adds poles to the overall system, it can be integrated into the control of such systems by supplying an otherwise unavailable state vector.

title: Trajectory Surface Hopping Approach to Nonadiabatic Molecular Collisions: The Reaction of H+ with D2
abstract: An extension of the classical trajectory approach is proposed that may be useful in treating many types of nonadiabatic molecular collisions. Nuclei are assumed to move classically on a single potential energy surface until an avoided surface crossing or other region of large nonadiabatic coupling is reached. At such points the trajectory is split into two branches, each of which follows a different potential surface. The validity of this model as applied to the HD2+ system is assessed by numerical integration of the appropriate semiclassical equations. A 3d “trajectory surface hopping” treatment of the reaction of H+ with D2 at a collision energy of 4 eV is reported. The excellent agreement with experiment is an encouraging indication of the potential usefulness of this approach.
summary:
Title: New Model for Analyzing Molecular Collisions Unveiled

In an innovative development in the field of semiclassical physics, researchers John C. Tully and Richard K. Preston have proposed a new technique called Trajectory Surface Hopping Approach. This method is intended to enhance the treatment of numerous nonadiabatic molecular collisions.

The approach works by following the classical movement of nuclei on a single potential energy surface until an avoided crossing or region of significant nonadiabatic coupling is encountered. At such points, the trajectory splits into two branches, each following a different potential surface. The validity and usefulness of this model are demonstrated through numerical integration of semiclassical equations, applied to the HD2+ system in a 3D context.

Preliminary results from applying this method to the reaction of H+ with D2 at a collision energy of 4 eV show excellent agreement with experimental data, signaling a promising avenue for future studies in molecular dynamics.

title: Probability of second law violations in shearing steady states
abstract: We propose a new definition of natural invariant measure for trajectory segments of finite duration for a many-particle system. On this basis we give an expression for the probability of fluctuations in the shear stress of a fluid in a nonequilibrium steady state far from equilibrium. In particular we obtain a formula for the ratio that, for a finite time, the shear stress reverse sign, violating the second law of thermodynamics. Computer simulations support this formula.

Remarkably, they derive a formula that estimates the likelihood of the shear stress reversing sign within a finite time frame, theoretically violating the second law of thermodynamics. Their findings are bolstered by computer simulations, hinting at significant shifts in understanding the mechanics and behavior of non-equilibrium systems.

abstract: This paper contains ground‐motion prediction equations (GMPEs) for average horizontal‐component ground motions as a function of earthquake magnitude, distance from source to site, local average shear‐wave velocity, and fault type. Our equations are for peak ground acceleration (PGA), peak ground velocity (PGV), and 5%‐damped pseudo‐absolute‐acceleration spectra (PSA) at periods between 0.01 s and 10 s . They were derived by empirical regression of an extensive strong‐motion database compiled by the “PEER NGA” (Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research Center's Next Generation Attenuation) project. For periods less than 1 s , the analysis used 1,574 records from 58 mainshocks in the distance range from 0 km to 400 km (the number of available data decreased as period increased). The primary predictor variables are moment magnitude ( M ), closest horizontal distance to the surface projection of the fault plane ( R JB ), and the time‐averaged shear‐wave velocity from the surface to 30 m ( V S30 ). The equations are applicable for M =5–8, R JB <200 km , and V S30 =180–1300 m/s.
summary:
Scientific Paper Offers New Ground-Motion Prediction Equations

A new study published in Earthquake Spectra, authored by David M. Boore and Gail M. Atkinson, presents ground-motion prediction equations (GMPEs) for peak ground acceleration (PGA), peak ground velocity (PGV), and 5%-damped pseudo-absolute-acceleration spectra (PSA). The research is significant in the fields of geodesy, seismology, and earthquake engineering.

The GMPEs, derived from a strong-motion database compiled by the Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research Center's Next Generation Attenuation (PEER NGA) project, focus on average horizontal-component ground motions as a function of earthquake magnitude, distance from source to site, local average shear-wave velocity, and fault type. This study covers periods between 0.01 s and 10 s, with the data analysis utilizing 1,574 records from 58 mainshocks in the distance range from 0 km to 400 km.

The primary predictor variables are moment magnitude (M), closest horizontal distance to the surface projection of the fault plane (RJB), and the time-averaged shear-wave velocity from the surface to 30m (Vs30). These equations are applicable for M=5–8, RJB<200 km, and Vs30=180-1300 m/s. The new GMPEs will play an essential role in improving earthquake risk assessment and seismic design standards for buildings and structures.

title: Monotone Comparative Statics
abstract: The authors derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the solution set of an optimization problem to be monotonic in the parameters of the problem. In addition, they develop practical methods for checking the condition and demonstrate its applications to the classical theories of the competitive firm, the monopolist, the Bertrand oligopolist, consumer and growth theory, game theory, and general equilibrium analysis. Copyright 1994 by The Econometric Society.
summary:
Title: Ground-breaking Study Clarifies Monotone Optimization Conditions for Economics

New research published in Econometrica offers an innovative solution to a longstanding challenge in mathematical economics: developing a necessary and sufficient condition for the monotonicity of an optimization problem's solution set regarding its parameters. According to Paul Milgrom and Chris Shannon, this advancement can enhance our understanding across various economic theories, from competitive markets and consumer behavior to game theory and general equilibrium analysis. By providing practical methods to verify this condition, the authors enable a more precise and efficient approach in evaluating economic models and their impact on decision-making processes.

title: Lorentz Invariance and the Gravitational Field
abstract: An argument leading from the Lorentz invariance of the Lagrangian to the introduction of the gravitational field is presented. Utiyama's discussion is extended by considering the 10-parameter group of inhomogeneous Lorentz transformations, involving variation of the coordinates as well as the field variables. It is then unnecessary to introduce a priori curvilinear coordinates or a Riemannian metric, and the new field variables introduced as a consequence of the argument include the vierbein components hkμ as well as the ``local affine connection'' Aijμ. The extended transformations for which the 10 parameters become arbitrary functions of position may be interpreted as general coordinate transformations and rotations of the vierbein system. The free Lagrangian for the new fields is shown to be a function of two covariant quantities analogous to Fμν for the electromagnetic field, and the simplest possible form is just the usual curvature scalar density expressed in terms of hkμ and Aijμ. This Lagrangian is of first order in the derivatives, and is the analog for the vierbein formalism of Palatini's Lagrangian. In the absence of matter, it yields the familiar equations Rμν=0 for empty space, but when matter is present there is a difference from the usual theory (first pointed out by Weyl) which arises from the fact that Aijμ appears in the matter field Lagrangian, so that the equation of motion relating Aijμ to hkμ is changed. In particular, this means that, although the covariant derivative of the metric vanishes, the affine connection Γλμν is nonsymmetric. The theory may be reexpressed in terms of the Christoffel connection, and in that case additional terms quadratic in the ``spin density'' Skij appear in the Lagrangian. These terms are almost certainly too small to make any experimentally detectable difference to the predictions of the usual metric theory.
summary:
New Mathematical Physics Paper Reveals Groundbreaking Argument on Gravitational Field

A groundbreaking argument linking Lorentz invariance with the introduction of the gravitational field has been presented by physicist T. W. B. Kibble, published in the Journal of Mathematical Physics. In this paper, Kibble extends Utiyama's discussion, considering a wide range of coordinated and field variable transformations.

In doing so, he introduces new field variables such as the vierbein components hkμ and the "local affine connection" Aijμ, eliminating the need for predetermined curvilinear coordinates or Riemannian metrics. The extended theory allows for greater flexibility, with the 10 parameters becoming arbitrary functions of position, interpretable as general coordinate transformations and rotations of the vierbein system.

This new Lagrangian, featuring covariant quantities akin to the electromagnetic field's Fμν, is first-order in derivatives and serves as an analog for the Palatini formalism in the context of the vierbein framework. The Lagrangian generates familiar equations for empty space (Rμν=0) but showcases differences when matter is present, which were initially pointed out by Weyl and stem from Aijμ's incorporation into the matter field Lagrangian. As a result, the affine connection Γλμν becomes nonsymmetric, even though the covariant derivative of the metric vanishes. The paper also suggests additional terms in the Lagrangian, which, while significant conceptually, may be too tiny to have any experimentally detectable impact on the predictions of the common metric theory.

title: Coefficient of Restitution Interpreted as Damping in Vibroimpact
abstract: During impact the relative motion of two bodies is often taken to be simply represented as half of a damped sine wave, according to the Kelvin-Voigt model. This is shown to be logically untenable, for it indicates that the bodies must exert tension on one another just before separating. Furthermore, it denotes that the damping energy loss is proportional to the square of the impacting velocity, instead of to its cube, as can be deduced from Goldsmith’s work. A damping term λxnx˙ is here introduced; for a sphere impacting a plate Hertz gives n = 3/2. The Kelvin-Voigt model is shown to be approximated as a special case deducible from this law, and applicable when impacts are absent. Physical experiments have confirmed this postulate.
summary:
Headline: New Damping Model Challenges Traditional Impact Analysis in Physics

Summary:
A new damping interpretation in vibroimpact challenges the Kelvin-Voigt model, traditionally used to represent impacts as half a damped sine wave. According to a paper by K. H. Hunt and F.R.E. Crossley published in the Journal of Applied Mechanics, this model suggests that bodies exert tension upon each other before separation and that damping energy loss is proportional to the square of impact velocity - contradicting Goldsmith's work which suggests a cubic relationship. The authors propose a new damping term, λxnx˙, and demonstrate that it can be derived from Hertz's spherical impact law in classical mechanics. Physical experiments support this postulate, marking a significant departure from existing impact analysis models.
topic: Dynamics and Control of Mechanical Systems

title: Hydrodynamic fluctuations at the convective instability
abstract: The effects of thermal fluctuations on the convective instability are considered. It is shown that the Langevin equations for hydrodynamic fluctuations are equivalent, near the instability, to a model for the crystallization of a fluid in equilibrium. Unlike the usual models, however, the free energy of the present system does not possess terms cubic in the order parameter, and therefore the system undergoes a second-order transition in mean-field theory. The effects of fluctuations on such a model were recently discussed by Brazovskii, who found a first-order transition in three dimensions. A similar argument also leads to a discontinuous transition for the convective model, which behaves two dimensionally for sufficiently large lateral dimensions. The magnitude of the jump is unobservably small, however, because of the weakness of the thermal fluctuations being considered. The relation of the present analysis to the work of Graham and Pleiner is discussed.
summary:
Title: New Insights on Convective Instability: A Second-Order Transition Approach

In a groundbreaking paper published in Physical Review A, J. B. Swift and P. C. Hohenberg propose a new perspective on convective instability in physics. They suggest that hydrodynamic fluctuations near the instability are analogous to the crystallization of a fluid in equilibrium, unlike previous models which often feature cubic terms in the order parameter.

Their model, devoid of these cubic terms, predicts a second-order transition in mean-field theory, contrasting with the first-order transition found by Brazovskii in three dimensions. However, due to the weakness of the thermal fluctuations under consideration, the magnitude of the transition jump is too minuscule to observe.

The authors also discuss their work in relation to that of Graham and Pleiner, adding another crucial piece to the puzzle of understanding convective instability and its consequences.

title: A 20th century acceleration in global sea‐level rise
abstract: Multi‐century sea‐level records and climate models indicate an acceleration of sea‐level rise, but no 20th century acceleration has previously been detected. A reconstruction of global sea level using tide‐gauge data from 1950 to 2000 indicates a larger rate of rise after 1993 and other periods of rapid sea‐level rise but no significant acceleration over this period. Here, we extend the reconstruction of global mean sea level back to 1870 and find a sea‐level rise from January 1870 to December 2004 of 195 mm, a 20th century rate of sea‐level rise of 1.7 ± 0.3 mm yr −1 and a significant acceleration of sea‐level rise of 0.013 ± 0.006 mm yr −2 . This acceleration is an important confirmation of climate change simulations which show an acceleration not previously observed. If this acceleration remained constant then the 1990 to 2100 rise would range from 280 to 340 mm, consistent with projections in the IPCC TAR.
summary:
Title: New Study Finds Decade-Long Sea Level Rise Acceleration Confirms Climate Change Fears

Subtitle: Research led by John Church and Neil White of the Antarctic Climate & Ecosystem Cooperative Research Centre published in Geophysical Research Letters reveals a significant acceleration in global sea level rise in the 20th century, providing important confirmation for climate change simulations and echoing warnings from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

Summary: Previous research had not detected any sea level rise acceleration during the 20th century. However, a new study extending back to 1870 reveals that over this period, global sea levels have risen at an average rate of 1.7 mm/year (overall 195 mm). The new analysis also shows a significant acceleration in sea level rise towards the end of the 20th century that may indicate increasingly rapid climatic changes—a finding critical to understanding and predicting future sea level impacts and implications for coastal communities worldwide.

title: Kinematics of the western Mediterranean
abstract: Summary The kinematic understanding of the relationship between relative plate motion and the structure of orogenic belts depends upon a knowledge of relative plate motion across the plate boundary system, the relative motion of small blocks and flakes within the system, an evaluation of orogenic body forces, and an understanding of the thermomechanical evolution of the upper part of the orogenic lithosphere in determining strength and detachment levels. We have built a preliminary model for the Cenozoic kinematic evolution of the western Mediterranean oceanic basins and their peripheral orogens that integrates (1) the motion of Africa relative to Europe based upon a new study of Atlantic fracture zones using SEASAT data and the Lamont-Doherty magnetic anomaly database, (2) a new interpretation of the rotation of Corsica/Sardinia and the opening of the Balearic and Tyrrhenian oceanic basins, (3) sedimentary facies sequences in the Apennines, Calabria, and Sicily, and (4) Apennine/Calabrian structure and structural sequence.
summary:
Headline: New Model Unveils Cenozoic Kinematic Evolution of Western Mediterranean Basins

In a new study published in Geological Society London Special Publications, researchers led by John Dewey, Mark Helman, Steven D. Knott, Eugenio Turco, and D. H. W. Hutton have constructed a preliminary model that sheds light on the dynamic evolution of Western Mediterranean oceanic basins and their adjacent orogenic belts over the Cenozoic Era.

The groundbreaking work integrates various elements including Africa's motion relative to Europe, derived from a new study of Atlantic fracture zones using SEASAT data and the Lamont-Doherty magnetic anomaly database; a novel interpretation of Corsica/Sardinia rotation and the opening of the Balearic and Tyrrhenian oceanic basins; sedimentary facies sequences in the Apennines, Calabria, and Sicily; and an analysis of the Apennine/Calabrian structure and structural sequence. This comprehensive approach aims to deepen our understanding of plate motion kinematics and the development of orogenic belts within the Mediterranean region.

title: General Relativistic Fluid Spheres
abstract: In Part I of this paper certain well known results concerning the Schwarzschild interior solution are generalized to more general static fluid spheres in the form of inequalities comparing the boundary value of ${g}_{44}$ with certain expressions involving only the mass concentration and the ratio of the central energy density to the central pressure. A minimal theorem appropriate to the relativistic domain is derived for the central pressure, corresponding to a well-known classical result. Inequalities involving the proper energy and the potential energy are also considered, as is the introduction of the physical radius in place of the coordinate radius. A singularity-free elementary algebraic solution of the field equations is presented and exact values obtained from it compared with the limits prescribed by some of the inequalities. In Part II an answer is given to the question whether the total amount of radiation emitted during the symmetrical gravitational contraction of an amount of matter whose initial energy, at complete dispersion, is ${W}_{0}$ can ever exceed ${W}_{0}$.
summary:
**Newtonian Static Spheres Reimagined in General Relativity: Paper Offers Radiant Solution**

In a groundbreaking study published in Physical Review, renowned physicist H. A. Buchdahl has offered an exciting evolution of Newtonian static spheres into the realm of general relativity.

The paper, titled "General Relativistic Fluid Spheres," generalizes well-known results about the Schwarzschild interior solution. By introducing inequalities comparing the boundary value of ${g}_{44}$ with expressions involving only mass concentration and the ratio of central energy density to pressure, Buchdahl brings forth a new minimal theorem within the relativistic domain.

The work also delves into the comparison between proper and potential energy, introduces the physical radius in lieu of coordinate radius, and presents an elementary algebraic solution void of singularities. Exact values derived from this solution are compared against inequalities to establish their relevance and validity.

In Part II, Buchdahl answers a longstanding question about the maximum amount of radiation emitted during symmetrical gravitational contraction of matter, providing crucial insights on the limits of energy emissions within general relativity.

title: Quantum Field Theory in Curved Space-Time and Black Hole Thermodynamics
abstract: In this book, Robert Wald provides a coherent, pedagogical introduction to the formulation of quantum field theory in curved spacetime. He begins with a treatment of the ordinary one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator, progresses through the construction of quantum field theory in flat spacetime to possible constructions of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, and, ultimately, to an algebraic formulation of the theory. In his presentation, Wald disentangles essential features of the theory from inessential ones (such as a particle interpretation) and clarifies relationships between various approaches to the formulation of the theory. He also provides a comprehensive, up-to-date account of the Unruh effect, the Hawking effect, and some of its ramifications. In particular, the subject of black hole thermodynamics, which remains an active area of research, is treated in depth. This book will be accessible to students and researchers who have had introductory courses in general relativity and quantum field theory, and will be of interest to scientists in general relativity and related fields.
summary:
**Headline:**
New Book Offers Comprehensive Introduction to Quantum Field Theory in Curved Spacetime

**Summary:**
In a new book, physicist Robert Wald offers an accessible and pedagogical guide to the intricate field of quantum field theory in curved spacetime. The work serves as a bridge between quantum gravity and general relativity, providing a clear path from foundational concepts like quantum harmonic oscillators, to complex theories that could aid our understanding of black holes and their thermodynamics. Key topics such as the Unruh effect, Hawking effect, and related ramifications are also explored in depth, making this book an essential read for students and researchers with backgrounds in these fields. The study aims to clarify relationships between various approaches to quantum field theory, and its insights will undoubtedly spark further research in the active area of black hole thermodynamics.

title: An introduction to the theory of diffusive shock acceleration of energetic particles in tenuous plasmas
abstract: The central idea of diffusive shock acceleration is presented from microscopic and macroscopic viewpoints; applied to reactionless test particles in a steady plane shock the mechanism is shown to produce a power law spectrum in momentum with a slope which, to lowest order in the ratio of plasma to particle speed, depends only on the compression in the shock. The associated time scale is found (also by a macroscopic and a microscopic method) and the problems of spherical shocks, as exemplified by a point explosion and a stellar-wind terminator, are treated by singular perturbation theory. The effect of including the particle reaction is then studied. It is shown that if the scattering is due to resonant waves these can rapidly grow with unknown consequences. The possible steady modified shock structures are classified and generalised Rankine-Hugoniot conditions found. Modifications of the spectrum are discussed on the basis of an exact, if rather artificial, solution, a high-energy asymptotic expansion and a perturbation expansion due to Blandford. It is pointed out that no steady solution can exist for very strong shocks; the possible time dependence is briefly discussed.
summary:
Paper introduces theory on diffusive shock acceleration of energetic particles in tenuous plasmas
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

In an article published in *Reports on Progress in Physics*, physicist L. O'C Drury presents a comprehensive introduction to the study of diffusive shock acceleration, addressing both microscopic and macroscopic viewpoints. Focusing on reactionless test particles in steady plane shocks, this theory produces power law spectra with slopes depending on the compression in the shock.

Using two different methods, Drury also determines the associated time scale for these processes. The paper then explores the problems of spherical shocks using singular perturbation theories. Additionally, it examines the impact of particle reactions and shows that resonant waves can grow quickly, with potential unknown consequences. Finally, modified shock structures are classified, and generalized Rankine-Hugoniot conditions are presented.

The paper notes that no steady solution can exist for very strong shocks and briefly discusses possible time dependencies. The study builds upon the foundations of classical mechanics and plasma physics to investigate how shock waves in tenuous plasmas accelerate energetic particles, shedding light on various space phenomena involving such interactions.

title: Motility-Induced Phase Separation
abstract: Self-propelled particles include both self-phoretic synthetic colloids and various microorganisms. By continually consuming energy, they bypass the laws of equilibrium thermodynamics. These laws enforce the Boltzmann distribution in thermal equilibrium: The steady state is then independent of kinetic parameters. In contrast, self-propelled particles tend to accumulate where they move more slowly. They may also slow down at high density for either biochemical or steric reasons. This creates positive feedback, which can lead to motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) between dense and dilute fluid phases. At leading order in gradients, a mapping relates variable-speed, self-propelled particles to passive particles with attractions. This deep link to equilibrium phase separation is confirmed by simulations but generally breaks down at higher order in gradients: New effects, with no equilibrium counterpart, then emerge. We give a selective overview of the fast-developing field of MIPS, focusing on theory and simulation but including a brief speculative survey of its experimental implications.
summary:
In "Motility-Induced Phase Separation," physicists Michael E. Cates and Julien Tailleur delve into an intriguing area of research that examines self-propelled particles like synthetic colloids and microorganisms, which defy the principles of thermal equilibrium due to continuous energy consumption. Unlike thermal equilibrium where particles evenly distribute according to Boltzmann's distribution, self-propelled particles tend to concentrate in slower-moving areas, leading to a positive feedback loop that can result in motility-induced phase separation (MIPS).

The research offers a theoretical link between variable-speed self-propelled particles and passive particles with attractions. Simulations support this relationship but at higher gradient levels, unique effects devoid of any equilibrium counterpart surface. This review provides an overview of the rapidly evolving field of MIPS, emphasizing theory and simulations while also exploring potential experimental implications, offering a glimpse into the intriguing world of self-propelled particles behavior in fluids.
journal: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics

title: Time-dependent approach to semiclassical dynamics
abstract: In this paper we develop a new approach to semiclassical dynamics which exploits the fact that extended wavefunctions for heavy particles (or particles in harmonic potentials) may be decomposed into time−dependent wave packets, which spread minimally and which execute classical or nearly classical trajectories. A Gaussian form for the wave packets is assumed and equations of motion are derived for the parameters characterizing the Gaussians. If the potential (which may be nonseparable in many coordinates) is expanded in a Taylor series about the instantaneous center of the (many−particle) wave packet, and up to quadratic terms are kept, we find the classical parameters of the wave packet (positions, momenta) obey Hamilton’s equation of motion. Quantum parameters (wave packet spread, phase factor, correlation terms, etc.) obey similar first order quantum equations. The center of the wave packet is shown to acquire a phase equal to the action integral along the classical path. State−specific quantum information is obtained from the wave packet trajectories by use of the superposition principle and projection techniques. Successful numerical application is made to the collinear He + H2 system widely used as a test case. Classically forbidden transitions are accounted for and obtained in the same manner as the classically allowed transitions; turning points present no difficulties and flux is very nearly conserved.
summary:
Title: New Framework Unveiled for Semiclassical Dynamics Exploiting Wave Packets

Subheading: Physics Breakthrough Could Simplify Complex Quantum Systems

In a groundbreaking study published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, renowned physicist Eric J. Heller presents a novel time-dependent approach to semiclassical dynamics. This new approach exploits the properties of wave packets—minimally spreading entities that exhibit classical or near-classical behavior—to understand and analyze complex quantum systems more efficiently.

The study assumes a Gaussian form for these wave packets, allowing for the derivation of equations of motion for the parameters characterizing the Gaussians. The author also demonstrates how this new framework can account for "classically-forbidden" transitions and conserve energy flux, making it significantly useful in analyzing various physical situations. The method's success is demonstrated through its application to the collinear He + H2 system, a widely recognized benchmark case within physics research.

title: The Particle Problem in the General Theory of Relativity
abstract: The writers investigate the possibility of an atomistic theory of matter and electricity which, while excluding singularities of the field, makes use of no other variables than the ${g}_{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}}$ of the general relativity theory and the ${\ensuremath{\phi}}_{\ensuremath{\mu}}$ of the Maxwell theory. By the consideration of a simple example they are led to modify slightly the gravitational equations which then admit regular solutions for the static spherically symmetric case. These solutions involve the mathematical representation of physical space by a space of two identical sheets, a particle being represented by a "bridge" connecting these sheets. One is able to understand why no neutral particles of negative mass are to be found. The combined system of gravitational and electromagnetic equations are treated similarly and lead to a similar interpretation. The most natural elementary charged particle is found to be one of zero mass. The many-particle system is expected to be represented by a regular solution of the field equations corresponding to a space of two identical sheets joined by many bridges. In this case, because of the absence of singularities, the field equations determine both the field and the motion of the particles. The many-particle problem, which would decide the value of the theory, has not yet been treated.
summary:
Headline: Einstein and Rosen Propose New Theory of Matter and Electricity in 'The Particle Problem'

Summary:
In a groundbreaking paper published in Physical Review, physicists Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen explore an atomistic theory that avoids field singularities while only utilizing the ${g}_{\ensuremath{\mu}\ensuremath{\nu}}$ from general relativity theory and the ${\ensuremath{\phi}}_{\ensuremath{\mu}}$ from Maxwell theory. By examining a simple case, they slightly modify gravitational equations to accommodate regular solutions for spherically symmetric static cases. These solutions depict physical space as two identical sheets, with particles represented by "bridges" connecting them. The article also suggests that neutral particles of negative mass are non-existent and the most natural elementary charged particle is zero-mass. Though the many-particle problem, crucial to determining the theory's validity, remains unsolved, this study lays essential groundwork for understanding the relationship between gravity and electromagnetism at a fundamental level.

title: On the stability of crystal lattices. I
abstract: The stability of lattices is discussed from the standpoint of the method of small vibrations. It is shown that it is not necessary to determine the whole vibrational spectrum, but only its long wave part. The stability conditions are nothing but the positive definiteness of the macroscopic deformation energy, and can be expressed in the form of inequalities for the elastic constants. A new method is explained for calculating these as lattice sums, and this method is applied to the three monatomic lattice types assuming central forces. In this way one obtains a simple explanation of the fact that the face-centred lattice is stable, whereas the simple lattice is always unstable and the body-centred also except for small exponents of the attractive forces. It is indicated that this method might be used for an improvement of the, at present, rather unsatisfactory theory of strength.
summary: In a groundbreaking study published in Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, physicist Max Born delves into the stability of crystal lattices using the method of small vibrations. The paper, titled "On the stability of crystal lattices. I," offers a breakthrough solution for determining only the long wave part of the vibrational spectrum instead of the entire spectrum to establish stability conditions. Through this pioneering approach, Born establishes that the macroscopic deformation energy's positive definiteness is key to crystalline lattice stability. Using a novel method to calculate elastic constants as lattice sums, Born explores the three common monatomic lattices and reveals why the face-centred lattice shows stability over other types like simple and body-centred lattices (except for small exponents of attractive forces). The paper also hints at the potential enhancement of current theories on the strength of crystalline materials, a significant step towards a more robust understanding of their behavior under stress.

summary:
**New Research Explores the Evolution of Compressible Fluid Dynamics**

John Anderson's latest paper, "Modern Compressible Flow: With Historical Perspective," delves deep into the mechanics of compressible flow, a central concept in modern physics. The study traces the evolution and offers insights into influential ideas like inviscid flows, transonic flow, and compressible flow.

The work builds upon significant prior work, exploring integral forms of conservation equations for inviscid flows, one-dimensional flow, oblique shock waves, and unsteady wave motion. It also presents a time-marching technique with applications to supersonic blunt bodies, nozzles, and three-dimensional flow. Additionally, the paper discusses transonic flow, hypersonic flow, high-temperature gas properties, and high-temperature flows' essential examples.

This extensive work aims to support a better understanding of compressible fluid dynamics – from fundamental equations to practical applications, providing valuable resources for engineers and scientists working in this field.

abstract: Modern Quantum Mechanics is a classic graduate level textbook, covering the main quantum mechanics concepts in a clear, organized and engaging manner. The second edition, revised by Jim Napolitano, introduces topics that extend the text's usefulness into the twenty-first century, such as advanced mathematical techniques associated with quantum mechanical calculations, while at the same time retaining classic developments such as neutron interferometer experiments, Feynman path integrals, correlation measurements, and Bell's inequality. title: A Simple Theory of the Survey Response: Answering Questions versus Revealing Preferences
abstract: Opinion research is beset by two major types of artifactual variance: huge amounts of overtime response instability and the common tendency for seemingly trivial changes in questionnaire form to affect the expression of attitudes. We propose a simple model that converts this anomalous ; error variance into sources of substantive insight into the nature of public opinion. The model abandons the conventional but implausible notion that most people possess opinions at the level of specificity of typical survey items-and instead assumes that most people are internally conflicted over most political issues-and that most respond to survey questions on the basis of whatever ideas are at the top of their heads at the moment of answering. Numerous empirical regularities are shown to be consistent with these assumptions.
summary:
Paper Title: Unraveling Public Opinion's Mysteries - A New Model for Survey Response

In the American Journal of Political Science, authors John Zaller and Stanley Feldman present a novel theory that could revolutionize opinion research. The study addresses the pervasive issue of artifactual variance, which includes significant overtime response instability and questionnaire-related attitude expression changes.

The new model transforms these problematic sources of error variance into valuable insights about the complexities of public opinion. Abandoning the traditional notion that most people have concrete opinions for every survey question, the model proposes instead that individuals often have conflicting views on political issues and respond to questions based on their immediate thoughts at the moment of answering.

Numerous empirical regularities are demonstrated as consistent with these assumptions, providing a fresh perspective on the intricate workings of public opinion. This groundbreaking theory could lead to more accurate representations of people's attitudes and opinions in surveys.

abstract: A computer simulation model, FARSITE, includes existing fire behavior models for surface, crown, spotting, point-source fire acceleration, and fuel moisture. summary: In a significant contribution to wildfire research, a new computer simulation model, FARSITE, has been developed by scientist Mark A. Finney. The model combines multiple existing fire behavior models, including surface, crown, and spotting fires, as well as point-source fire acceleration and fuel moisture. In the latest publication from Ray W. Clough, Joseph Penzien, and D. S. Griffin in the Journal of Applied Mechanics, the team presents a comprehensive guide on structural dynamics analysis. title: Fitts' Law as a Research and Design Tool in Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: According to Fitts' law, human movement can be modeled by analogy to the transmission of information. Fitts' popular model has been widely adopted in numerous research areas, including kinematics, human factors, and (recently) human-computer interaction (HCI). The present study provides a historical and theoretical context for the model, including an analysis of problems that have emerged through the systematic deviation of observations from predictions. Refinements to the model are described, including a formulation for the index of task difficulty that is claimed to be more theoretically sound than Fitts' original formulation. The model's utility in predicting the time to position a cursor and select a target is explored through a review of six Fitts' law studies employing devices such as the mouse, trackball, joystick, touchpad, helmet-mounted sight, and eye tracker. An analysis of the performance measures reveals tremendous inconsistencies, making across-study comparisons difficult. Sources of experimental variation are identified to reconcile these differences.
summary:
In the realm of human-computer interaction, scientist I. Scott MacKenzie revisits Fitts' Law, a widely recognized model for predicting human movement, in a new study published in Human-Computer Interaction. Fitts' Law is historically significant as it analogizes human movement to information transmission, finding application in diverse fields such as kinematics and human factors.

However, MacKenzie's paper highlights challenges faced when applying this model in recent HCI research, reporting discrepancies between observed findings and predictions. The paper offers refinements to the model, proposing a more robust index of task difficulty, and presents the results from six studies that employed various input devices like mice, joysticks, and eye trackers. The study aims to establish consistency across studies, addressing variances caused by experimental factors and providing guidance for future HCI research utilizing Fitts' Law.

title: The holographic principle
abstract: There is strong evidence that the area of any surface limits the information content of adjacent spacetime regions, at $1.4\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}{10}^{69}$ bits per square meter. This article reviews the developments that have led to the recognition of this entropy bound, placing special emphasis on the quantum properties of black holes. The construction of light sheets, which associate relevant spacetime regions to any given surface, is discussed in detail. This article explains how the bound is tested, and its validity is demonstrated in a wide range of examples. A universal relation between geometry and information is thus uncovered. It has yet to be explained. The holographic principle asserts that its origin must lie in the number of fundamental degrees of freedom involved in a unified description of spacetime and matter. It must be manifest in an underlying quantum theory of gravity. This article surveys some successes and challenges in implementing the holographic principle.
summary:
Headline: "The Holographic Principle in Physics: The Quantum Connection Between Space, Time, and Information"

Summary:
In a seminal work published in Reviews of Modern Physics, Raphael Bousso delves into the intriguing 'Holographic Principle.' This principle proposes that the information content of adjacent spacetime regions is limited by the area of any surface, with each square meter carrying approximately $1.4\ifmmode\times\else\texttimes\fi{}{10}^{69}$ bits of data. The article provides a comprehensive review of the developments leading to this intriguing entropy bound, placing significant focus on the quantum properties of black holes. Bousso discusses the construction of light sheets, which link relevant spacetime regions to any given surface. The paper also explains how this bound is tested and demonstrates its validity across various examples. Ultimately, the Holographic Principle hints at a universal relation between geometry and information. However, its origins remain unexplained. The principle asserts that it lies in the number of fundamental degrees of freedom involved in a unified description of spacetime and matter, implying it will be crucial in any underlying quantum theory of gravity. The article surveys some successes and challenges in implementing the Holographic Principle, offering a fascinating perspective on the interplay between space, time, and information in physics.

title: Dislocations and Cracks in Anisotropic Elasticity
abstract: The solution of the elastic equations is considered for the case in which the state of the solid is independent of one of the three Cartesian coordinates. The stresses due to a dislocation, a wall of parallel dislocations, and a crack in an arbitrary non-uniform stress field are obtained. The results hold for the most general anisotropy in which no symmetry elements of the crystal are assumed.
summary:
Title: Revolutionary Discovery Advancing Crystalline Stress Analysis

In a groundbreaking paper published in the Philosophical Magazine, American mathematician A.N. Stroh presents a significant leap in understanding stress fields within anisotropic solids. This research focuses on cases where the state of the solid remains independent of one specific Cartesian coordinate, a concept fundamental to modern physics and mathematics. The findings offer solutions for elastic equations surrounding dislocations, walled dislocation arrays, and cracks – even in stress fields with arbitrary non-uniformities and complex anisotropies. This work marks a crucial step towards more accurate analysis of crystalline structures and their behavior under various stress conditions.

title: A Study of Locking Phenomena in Oscillators
abstract: Impression of an external signal upon an oscillator of similar fundamental frequency affects both the instantaneous amplitude and instantaneous frequency. Using the assumption that time constants in the oscillator circuit are small compared to the length of one beat cycle, a differential equation is derived which gives the oscillator phase as a function of time. With the aid of this equation, the transient process of "pull-in" as well as the production of a distorted beat note are described in detail. It is shown that the same equation serves to describe the motion of a pendulum suspended in a viscous fluid inside a rotating container. The whole range of locking phenomena is illustrated with the aid of this simple mechanical model.
summary:
Paper Title: Novel Insights into Locking Phenomena in Oscillators and Pendulums

In the Proceedings of the IRE, physicist R. Adler delves into the intricate world of beat phenomena in oscillators, a concept fundamental to acoustics. The study shows that an external signal can impact both the instantaneous amplitude and frequency of an oscillator with a similar fundamental frequency.

Adler presents a groundbreaking differential equation that describes the oscillator's phase as a function of time, enabling detailed exploration of the "pull-in" process and the production of a distorted beat note. Remarkably, the same equation is also found to be applicable in explaining the motion of a pendulum suspended in a viscous fluid inside a rotating container.

This research offers valuable insights into the locking phenomena observed in oscillators and pendulums, providing a simple yet effective mechanical model for understanding these complex interactions.

title: Kinetics of swelling of gels
abstract: We present a theory of the kinetics of the swelling of a gel. The characteristic time of swelling is proportional to the square of a linear dimension of the gel and is also proportional to the diffusion coefficient of the gel network, which is defined as D=E/f where E is the longitudinal bulk modulus of the network, and f is the coefficient of friction between the network and the gel fluid. This constitutes an essential difference between the present theory and the previous theory which is based on the assumption that the swelling time is determined by the diffusion coefficient of the fluid molecules. Experimental data are shown for spheres of 5% polyacrylamide gels and are analyzed using the present theory. The value of the diffusion coefficient obtained from the macroscopic swelling experiments shows excellent agreement with that obtained microscopically using laser light scattering spectroscopy.
summary:
Scientific Findings: Revolutionary Theory Offered on Swelling Dynamics of Gels

A groundbreaking study by researchers Toyoichi Tanaka and David J. Fillmore, published in The Journal of Chemical Physics, has unveiled a new theory regarding the kinetics of gel swelling. The research suggests that the swelling time is proportionate to the square of a gel's linear dimension and dependent on its diffusion coefficient—a parameter defined by the gel network’s longitudinal bulk modulus and friction coefficient. This theory diverges from previous assumptions focusing on fluid molecule diffusion coefficients, marking an essential advancement in materials science and thermodynamics research. The findings were corroborated through experiments conducted on spheres of 5% polyacrylamide gels. The study's diffusion coefficient values show remarkable agreement between macroscopic swelling experiments and microscopic measurements using laser light scattering spectroscopy, demonstrating the theory's applicability.

title: Cosmological Perturbation Theory
abstract: The linear perturbation theory of spatially homogeneous and isotropic universes is reviewed and reformulated extensively. In the first half of the article, a gauge-invariant formulation of the theory is carried out with special attention paid to the geometrical meaning of the perturbation. In the second half of the article, the application of the theory to some important cosmological models is discussed.

Summary:
In a groundbreaking study published in Progress of Theoretical Physics Supplement, renowned physicists Hideo Kodama and Misao Sasaki have reviewed and significantly extended the linear perturbation theory for spatially homogeneous and isotropic universes. This intriguing work focuses on developing a gauge-invariant formulation that provides a better understanding of the geometric implications of these cosmic perturbations. In addition, the researchers discuss the application of their reformulated theory to key cosmological models, setting the stage for potential advancements in understanding the nature and evolution of our universe. This study builds upon prior work related to perturbation theory in both quantum mechanics and astronomy, particularly emphasizing the critical concept of isotropy.

title: Evidence from the motions of old stars that the Galaxy collapsed.
abstract: The (U, V, W)-velocity vectors for 221 well-observed dwarf stars have been used to compute the eccentricities and angular momenta of the galactic orbits in a model galaxy. It is shown that the eccentricity and the observed ultraviolet excess are strongly correlated. The stars with the largest excess (i.e., lowest metal abundance) are invariably moving in highly elliptical orbits, whereas stars with little or no excess move in nearly circular orbits. Correlations also exist between the ultraviolet excess and the W-velocity. Finally, the excess and the angnlar momentum are correlated; stars with large ultraviolet excesses have small angular momenta. These correlations are discussed in terms of the dynamics of a collapsing galaxy. The data require that the oldest stars were formed out of gas falling toward the galactic center in the radial direction and collapsing from the halo onto the plane. The collapse was very rapid and only a few times 108 years were required for the gas to attain circular orbits in equilibrium (i e., gravitational attraction balanced by centrifugal acceleration). The scale of the collapse is tentatively estimated to be at least 10 in the radial direction and 25 in the Z-direction. The initial contraction must have begun near the time of formation of the first stars, some 1010 years ago.
summary:
* Title: Evidence Suggests Galaxy Collapsed Faster Than Previously Thought
* New research by O. J. Eggen, D. Lynden–Bell, and Allan Sandage provides compelling evidence that our galaxy underwent a rapid collapse billions of years ago. Using data from 221 well-observed dwarf stars, the researchers found significant correlations between the eccentricity of stars' orbits, their ultraviolet excess (indicating low metal abundance), and their angular momenta, providing strong evidence for a collapsing galaxy. The rapid collapse occurred over approximately 10 million years, significantly faster than previous estimates, and likely brought the oldest stars toward the galactic center. This groundbreaking research offers new insights into the early evolution of our galaxy. (The Astrophysical Journal)
allAuthors: O. J. Eggen; D. Lynden–Bell; Allan Sandage

title: Relativistic Equations for Adiabatic, Spherically Symmetric Gravitational Collapse
abstract: The Einstein equations for a spherically symmetrical distribution of matter are studied. The matter is described by the stress-energy tensor of an ideal fluid (heat flow and radiation are therefore excluded). In this case, the Einstein equations give a generalization of the Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations of hydrostatic equilibrium so as to include an acceleration term and a contribution to the effective mass of a shell of matter arising from its kinetic energy. A second equation also appears in this time-dependent case; it gives the rate of change of an appropriate "total energy" $m(r, t)$ of each fluid sphere in terms of the work done on this sphere by the fluid surrounding it. These equations would be an appropriate starting point for a study of relativistic gravitational collapse in which an adiabatic equation of state more realistic than the $p=0$ form of Oppenheimer and Snyder could be used.
summary: In the realm of physics, researchers Charles W. Misner and David H. Sharp have presented work on new equations for a spherically symmetric gravitational collapse, in a paper published by Physical Review. The equations are an advancement from the conventional Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, now including additional terms that account for acceleration and the kinetic energy of matter shells. The researchers propose these refined equations as a stepping stone towards studying more complex scenarios of relativistic gravitational collapse, and they consider using a more realistic adiabatic equation of state in their studies.

title: Computer simulation of atomic-displacement cascades in solids in the binary-collision approximation
abstract: A comprehensive computer program has been developed for the simulation of atomic-displacement cascades in a variety of crystalline solids, using the binary-collision approximation to contruct the projectile trajectories. The atomic scattering is governed by the Moli\'ere potential.Impact-parameter-dependent inelastic losses are included using Firsov's theory. Thermal vibrations of the target atoms and crystal surfaces may be included. Permanent displacement of lattice atoms may be based on either an energy-threshold criterion or a Frenkel-pair-separation criterion. An extensive series of calculations has been made for cascades in the simple metals Cu, Fe, and Au, to test the effects on the results of many of the model parameters. When a displacement-threshold energy is used, the number of Frenkel pairs is found to be a linear function of that part of the primary recoil energy which remains as the kinetic energy of atoms. This result is independent of target temperature, of the presence or absence of inelastic energy losses, and of various details of the model. In contrast, when a separation criterion is used, the number of defects increases less rapidly than linearly. This effect is caused by increased recombination in the highly disturbed tracks of the energetic recoils. Agreement between theoretical and experimental estimates of the radiation damage produced by neutron irradiation of Cu is substantially improved in the latter model.
summary:
Scientists Develop Advanced Simulation Tool for Atomic Displacement Cascades

In a new study published in Physical review. B, Solid state, researchers Mark T. Robinson and Ian M. Torrens have created a comprehensive computer program that simulates atomic-displacement cascades in various crystalline solids. The tool employs the binary-collision approximation to construct projectile trajectories, with the atomic scattering governed by the Molière potential.

The study builds on prior work involving recoil mechanics and Firsov's theory of impact-parameter-dependent inelastic losses. The computer program considers factors such as thermal vibrations of target atoms and crystal surfaces and the permanent displacement of lattice atoms based on either an energy threshold or a Frenkel-pair separation criterion.

The team carried out extensive calculations for cascades in Cu, Fe, and Au to test the impact of model parameters. The results indicate that, when using a displacement-threshold energy, the number of Frenkel pairs is proportionate to the remaining kinetic energy of atoms, regardless of target temperature, inelastic energy losses, or modeling details. This finding contrasts with simulations based on a separation criterion, which show a slower increase in defects caused by increased recombination in energetic recoil tracks. The study's findings lead to improved agreement between theoretical and experimental estimates of radiation damage from neutron irradiation of Cu using the separation criterion model.
allAuthors: Mark T. Robinson; Ian M. Torrens
